Volunteers are supervised by a named employee, are not counted toward required staffing, and residents are never used as substitutes for required staff (22 CCR §87411).
The Administrator reviews job descriptions and personnel policies annually and whenever a classification changes (see GOV-03), and updates them with the dates of review.

responsibilities.duty: Approves job descriptions and personnel policies. Provides the funds needed for lawful wages, sick leave and staffing.
Writes and updates job descriptions. Hires, supervises and keeps the schedule. Gives the written reporting and hiring-condition notices.
Follow their job descriptions, sign the abuse-reporting acknowledgement and report abuse as mandated reporters.
Tracks minimum wage compliance and sick leave accruals and keeps personnel files.

documentation: Job description for each LIC 500 classification, including the Administrator and Awake Night Caregiver
Current staff schedule and LIC 500 showing matching positions, days and hours
Signed abuse-reporting acknowledgement for each employee
Signed written conditions-of-employment notice
Hiring screening checklist (education and experience)
Payroll and sick leave records
Employment counsel opinion for any live-in or 24-hour shift
Annual review log for job descriptions and personnel policies

policies.category: Section B - Supportive Documents (B1, B2, B4-B17 for RCFE; B3 and B18 do not apply)
policies.title: In-Service Training Plan, First Aid Cards and Orientation Certificate
policies.applies_to: Administrator, direct care staff, all personnel who assist residents, and the Licensee
policies.purpose: To set out how [AGENCY NAME] trains new and existing staff, how training is documented, and how first aid cards and the Component I orientation certificate are obtained and submitted with the application.
policies.policy:
[AGENCY NAME] provides initial and ongoing training to every person who assists residents with personal activities of daily living. Training meets HSC §1569.625, HSC §1569.626 and HSC §1569.69, and first aid training comes from a qualified provider (22 CCR §87411).

This policy meets LIC 281 item B6.1 (in-service training plan, new employee training). New direct care staff complete 40 hours of initial training. At least 20 hours are completed before working alone, and the remaining 20 hours within 4 weeks (HSC §1569.625). The first 20 hours include 6 hours of dementia care and 4 hours on postural supports, restricted health conditions and hospice. Total initial dementia training is 12 hours (HSC §1569.626). Training is led by qualified trainers, namely the Administrator, a trainer from an approved vendor or community college, or a licensed professional with relevant experience. The trainer's qualifications are kept in the personnel record (22 CCR §87411).

Medication assistance training (HSC §1569.69): for a facility of 15 or fewer residents, 10 hours initial training plus an exam, with 6 hours hands-on before assisting with any medication and 4 hours within 2 weeks. For a facility of 16 or more, 24 hours initial (16 hands-on, 8 within 4 weeks) plus an exam. Annual medication training is 8 hours.

This policy meets LIC 281 item B6.2 (ongoing training). Topics are: 20 hours of annual training for direct care staff, including 8 hours on dementia (HSC §1569.625, §1569.626); 4 hours on postural supports, restricted health conditions and hospice; medication assistance (8 hours yearly for staff who assist); personal rights; abuse reporting; infection control; emergency and disaster procedures; and other topics listed in the RCFE training regulations. The plan includes the Administrator's continuing education of 40 hours every 2 years, including 8 hours of dementia training (HSC §1569.616). Training is scheduled at least [FREQUENCY, e.g., monthly] and recorded on a sign-in sheet, and certificates are kept in the personnel file.

This policy meets LIC 281 item B16 (First Aid Card). All personnel who provide direct care and supervision hold a first aid card from a qualified provider such as the American Red Cross. Copies of first aid cards for the applicant and each administrator are submitted with the application, and CDSS verifies them.

This policy meets LIC 281 item B17 (Orientation Certificate). Proof of attendance at the Component I orientation is submitted with the application. The certificate expires 30 days after access, so it is downloaded and saved when completed.

definitions.definition: The 40 hours a new direct care employee must complete: 20 before working alone and 20 within 4 weeks of hire.
Ongoing training given to staff after initial training, including the annual 20-hour requirement.
The CDSS orientation for license applicants, for which a certificate of attendance is issued.
Supervised, practical training in assisting with self-administered medications, required before a staff member assists.

procedures: Before any direct care hire, the Administrator confirms the new employee's start-of-work status: criminal record clearance, TB screening and health report on file (see ST-02, ST-04).

On the first day, the Administrator schedules the first 20 hours of initial training, including 6 hours of dementia care and 4 hours on postural supports, restricted health conditions and hospice. The new employee does not work alone until these 20 hours are complete and documented.
The Administrator schedules the remaining 20 hours, so they are completed within 4 weeks of hire. The Administrator keeps a training calendar with the due date for each new employee.
Total initial dementia training is 12 hours (HSC §1569.626). The Administrator tracks the 6 hours inside the first 20 hours, and the remaining 6 hours within the 4-week window.

A new employee who will assist with medications completes medication assistance training: for a facility of 15 or fewer, 6 hands-on hours before assisting and 4 more within 2 weeks, plus the exam (HSC §1569.69). For a facility of 16 or more, the 24-hour course applies (16 hands-on, 8 within 4 weeks) plus the exam.

Each employee holds a first aid card from a qualified provider (American Red Cross or equivalent) before providing direct care, or has completed first aid within [TIMEFRAME REQUIRED BY LICENSING]. The Administrator copies the card and records the expiration date.
Trainers are qualified persons. The Administrator records each trainer's name and qualifications on the training record kept in the personnel file (22 CCR §87411).

The Administrator builds an annual training calendar (B6.2) listing topics, trainer, date and hours: 20 hours of annual training including 8 hours of dementia care, 4 hours on postural supports, restricted health conditions and hospice, 8 hours of medication assistance for staff who assist, and refresher topics.
Each training session has a sign-in sheet with date, topic, hours, trainer and signatures. The sheet is filed, and the hours are added to each employee's training log.

The Administrator checks the training logs quarterly to confirm that each employee is on track for 20 annual hours. Staff who fall behind are scheduled for catch-up sessions before their anniversary date.
The Administrator's continuing education (40 hours every 2 years, including 8 hours on dementia) is tracked on the CE log (see SB-02). Certificates are kept in the Administrator Qualification File.
Before the application is submitted, the applicant and each administrator submit copies of first aid cards (B16). The Licensee confirms each card is legible and in date.

The applicant completes the Component I orientation and downloads the certificate right away because access expires after 30 days. The Licensee saves a PDF and a paper copy and includes the certificate in the application (B17).
The Licensee attaches this training plan to the Plan of Operation (see SB-05) and confirms on the FC-01 checklist that first aid cards and the orientation certificate are included.
The Administrator reviews the training plan each year (GOV-03) and updates it for any change in law or resident population, including added dementia needs.

responsibilities.duty: Schedules and documents all training, ensures trainers are qualified, keeps first aid cards current, and completes personal CE hours.
Complete required initial and annual hours, pass medication exams where applicable, and keep first aid cards valid.
Completes the Component I orientation and submits the certificate and first aid card copies with the application.
Delivers content as scheduled, signs attendance records and supplies completion certificates.

documentation: New-employee training plan and per-employee 40-hour initial training record
Annual training calendar and sign-in sheets
Individual training logs showing annual hours and dementia hours
Medication assistance training records and exam results
Trainer qualification records
Copies of first aid cards for staff, applicant and administrators
Component I orientation certificate (downloaded within the 30-day access window)
Administrator CE certificates

policies.category: Section B - Supportive Documents (B1, B2, B4-B17 for RCFE; B3 and B18 do not apply)
policies.title: Program Description and Plan of Operation
policies.applies_to: Licensee, Administrator, all staff
policies.purpose: To describe the purpose, services and day-to-day operation of [AGENCY NAME], so that licensing staff, residents and families understand what the facility provides and how it responds to emergencies, incidents and complaints.
policies.policy:
[AGENCY NAME] keeps a written Plan of Operation that covers purposes and goals, the admission agreement and admission policies, administrative organization, staffing and training, transportation, handling of resident money, the visiting policy, the approach to resident behavioral expression, and the infection control plan (22 CCR §87208). The plan includes dimensioned sketches. This Program Description is part of the plan. If it is issued as a pamphlet, the pamphlet must include every element B7.1-B7.11.

This policy meets LIC 281 item B7.1 (purpose, goals and program methods). [AGENCY NAME]'s philosophy is [PROGRAM PHILOSOPHY STATEMENT]. In general, [AGENCY NAME] supports residents' dignity, independence and choice in a safe, home-like setting. Residents receive care and supervision matched to individual needs and personal rights are respected.

This policy meets LIC 281 item B7.2 (days and hours of operation). [AGENCY NAME] operates 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, 365 days a year. Business and visiting hours are [HOURS].

This policy meets LIC 281 items B7.3 and B7.4 (daily schedule and one-month activity schedule). The daily schedule and the monthly calendar of social, educational and recreational activities each name who plans, who conducts and who assists residents to take part. The Activity Coordinator [or Administrator] plans activities. Direct care staff conduct and assist. Volunteers and outside providers assist under supervision. The calendar is posted and updated monthly. See DL-02.

This policy meets LIC 281 item B7.5 (basic services). Basic services follow the Department's guideline on basic services (LIC 604 or 604A) and include a room, three meals plus snacks, personal care and supervision, housekeeping, laundry, activities, assistance with self-administered medications, and arrangement of transportation, as set out in the admission agreement.

This policy meets LIC 281 item B7.6 (optional services). Optional services, if any, [LIST, e.g., additional laundry, beauty services, escort to appointments, special diets beyond basic] and their rates are listed in the admission agreement (see RR-03).

This policy meets LIC 281 item B7.7 (medical emergencies). When a resident becomes ill or injured, staff give first aid and call 9-1-1 for any imminent threat to health. Staff then notify the physician and the resident's designated person, and make required reports to CDSS (see SP-02, HS-03). A first aid kit is kept on site. Emergency numbers are posted and an ambulance number is readily available (22 CCR §87465). If the facility must evacuate, the Emergency Disaster Plan applies, including notice to the resident's hospice agency (22 CCR §87212; see SP-05).

This policy meets LIC 281 item B7.8 (self-administered medications). Staff only assist with self-administered medications. They do not give injections unless authorized by law and never force, hide or camouflage medications (22 CCR §87465). Medications are stored in a locked central place in the original container. See HS-01.

This policy meets LIC 281 item B7.9 (transportation). [AGENCY NAME] arranges transportation as described in DL-04, using [TRANSPORT ARRANGEMENT, e.g., facility vehicle, community paratransit, arranged medical transport], with the cost stated in the admission agreement.

This policy meets LIC 281 item B7.10 (community resources and consultants). [AGENCY NAME] uses the resources below. [LIST: local fire department, law enforcement, the Long-Term Care Ombudsman, local hospital, resident physicians, pharmacy, hospice and home health agencies, a registered dietitian, a nurse consultant, a medical transport provider, and the Area Agency on Aging.]

This policy meets LIC 281 item B7.11 (immediate response to incidents and complaints). Staff respond at once to any incident or complaint, protect safety, notify the Administrator, document the event the same shift, and report to CDSS and others as required. The procedure below is submitted for licensing approval.

definitions.definition: The written plan describing the facility's purpose, services, staffing, organization and operation, kept available for licensing review.
The services included in the base rate, as listed on the Department guideline (LIC 604 or 604A).
Services available for an added charge and listed in the admission agreement.
A medication the resident takes for themselves, with staff only assisting.

procedures: The Licensee writes the program philosophy (B7.1) and keeps it in the Plan of Operation. The Licensee reviews it with the Administrator at least yearly.
The Administrator states days and hours of operation (B7.2), 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, plus visiting and office hours, in the Plan of Operation and admission agreement.
The Administrator writes a daily activity schedule (B7.3) with times, activities and the title of the person who plans, conducts and assists with each.

The Activity Coordinator or designee prepares the monthly activity calendar (B7.4) before the start of each month with social, educational and recreational activities and the same planner/conductor/assistant information. The calendar is posted where residents can see it.
The Administrator lists the basic services (B7.5) based on the LIC 604/604A guideline and lists optional services and rates (B7.6) so that both match the admission agreement exactly.
During a medical emergency (B7.7), the staff member on duty stays with the resident, gives first aid within their training, and calls 9-1-1 for any imminent threat to health.

The staff member then notifies the resident's physician and the person responsible for the resident, and the Administrator. Notifications are written on the incident report the same shift. See SP-02 and HS-03.
Staff accompany or send with the resident the resident's face sheet, medication list and emergency information when the resident goes to the hospital.

For medications (B7.8), only staff who have completed medication assistance training assist residents. They check the label and resident name, provide the medication, and observe it being taken. They record it on the medication record. See HS-01.
Staff do not give injections unless authorized by law, and never force, hide or camouflage medications. Any refusal is documented and the physician or pharmacist is informed (22 CCR §87465).

The Administrator keeps a first aid kit and posts emergency numbers (9-1-1, poison control, physician, ambulance, CDSS, ombudsman, Administrator) in the common area and by the telephones (22 CCR §87465, §87212).
The Administrator documents transportation arrangements (B7.9), including who arranges rides, who pays and how residents request transportation. See DL-04.
The Administrator keeps a current list of community resources and consultants (B7.10) with names, services and phone numbers. The list is reviewed twice a year.
For immediate response to an incident or complaint (B7.11): the first staff member on the scene makes the resident safe, calls 9-1-1 if needed, and tells the Administrator right away.
The Administrator or designee investigates the same day, speaks with the resident and any witnesses, and takes steps to prevent recurrence.
The Administrator files the required reports to CDSS and others within the timeframes in SP-02 and REC-02, and answers any complaint in writing within [NUMBER] days per RR-02.
The Licensee reviews the whole Plan of Operation each year and whenever services change, and submits changes to CDSS as required. The review is recorded under GOV-03.

responsibilities.duty: Adopts the program description and approves changes. Ensures the Plan of Operation matches actual practice.
Maintains the Plan of Operation, schedules, transportation and resource lists. Directs incident and complaint response.
Plans the daily schedule and monthly calendar and arranges assistance for residents.
Respond to emergencies, assist with self-administered medications as trained, conduct activities and report incidents and complaints.

documentation: Plan of Operation including program philosophy and dimensioned sketches
Daily activity schedule and posted one-month activity calendar
List of basic and optional services (matching the admission agreement)
Medical emergency and medication assistance procedures
Transportation arrangement description
Community resource and consultant list
Incident and complaint response procedure and completed incident reports

policies.category: Section B - Supportive Documents (B1, B2, B4-B17 for RCFE; B3 and B18 do not apply)
policies.title: Admission Policies
policies.applies_to: Licensee, Administrator, admissions staff, direct care staff
policies.purpose: To set clear, lawful and consistent rules about who [AGENCY NAME] admits, how suitability is determined before admission, and what paperwork, disclosures and conditions apply. The policy ensures that no one is admitted whom the facility cannot safely serve.
policies.policy:
[AGENCY NAME] admits only persons whose needs it can meet within its license, program and staffing. The Plan of Operation (22 CCR §87208) includes these admission policies.

This policy meets LIC 281 item B9.1 (persons accepted for care). [AGENCY NAME] accepts persons [AGE RANGE, e.g., 60 years and older] who need care and supervision and whose needs fall within the acceptance and retention limits below. A compatibility determination is made when needed, considering the existing residents' needs, behaviors and room assignments, and never on a basis prohibited by 22 CCR §87468.1. Rates are in the admission agreement, and the refund policy is in RR-03. Acceptance and retention limits are in AD-03. The pre-admission appraisal, needs and services plan, medical assessment and admission agreement are covered below.

This policy meets LIC 281 item B9.2. Intake procedures for placement in group homes apply to group homes only. This item is not applicable to an RCFE.

This policy meets LIC 281 item B9.3 (criteria for assessing appropriateness of placement). Before admission, [AGENCY NAME] interviews the prospective resident, gathers the necessary paperwork, and determines suitability against the admission criteria (22 CCR §87457).

This policy meets LIC 281 items B9.7 (pre-admission appraisal plan), B9.4 (needs and services plan) and B9.6 (medical assessment). A pre-admission appraisal is completed with the resident's consent and covers functional, mental and social evaluation (22 CCR §87457). A needs and services plan is developed from the appraisal (see AD-02). A medical assessment by the resident's physician is obtained before admission. If the appraisal shows a hearing or other disability, LIC 9158 is completed (22 CCR §87507).

This policy meets LIC 281 item B9.5 (personal rights). Each resident and representative is told of the resident's personal rights (22 CCR §87468.1) at admission and in writing, and told that those rights will not be violated. [AGENCY NAME] will not deny admission or discriminate in transfer, discharge, room sharing, room or restroom assignment, preferred name or pronouns, or association on the basis of actual or perceived sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression or HIV status (22 CCR §87468.1(b)). The Department cannot waive this protection (§87468.1(d)).

Prohibited conditions: [AGENCY NAME] does not admit or retain a person who needs health services for, or has, stage 3 or 4 pressure injuries, a gastrostomy tube, a naso-gastric tube, staph or another serious infection, a tracheostomy, or total dependence on others for all activities of daily living. The list is not exhaustive (22 CCR §87615). See AD-03.

Admission agreement: a written agreement in 12-point type in plain language is signed and dated within 7 days of admission, and a copy is given immediately (22 CCR §87507). See RR-03.

This policy meets LIC 281 item B9.8 (emergency information). Each resident has current emergency contact information, physician, medication and allergy information, and preferred hospital on file at admission.

This policy meets LIC 281 item B9.9 (sign-in and sign-out). Residents sign out and in, or staff record departures and returns, so that staff know the whereabouts of residents in an emergency. Residents may leave at any time and are never locked in or prevented from leaving (22 CCR §87468.1). The sign-out record is for safety and does not restrict a resident's movement.

This policy meets LIC 281 item B9.10 (immunization requirements). At admission, [AGENCY NAME] requests the resident's immunization record and records it in the resident file. The facility follows its infection control policy (SP-07) and public health guidance on offering vaccinations. Declining a vaccine is a resident's right and is documented. A resident is not denied admission solely for an incomplete immunization record unless the law requires it.

This policy meets LIC 281 item B9.11 (physical examination requirements, including TB testing). Before admission, each resident provides a physician's report on the Department's required form, including a physical examination and TB test result or clearance.

definitions.definition: The interview and functional, mental and social evaluation, with the resident's consent, to decide whether the facility can meet the resident's needs before admission.
The written plan of the care and services the resident will receive, based on the appraisal.
A condition listed in 22 CCR §87615 that bars admission or retention.
The review of whether a new resident's needs and behaviors fit with the current residents' needs and the facility's program.

procedures: When an inquiry arrives, the Administrator or admissions designee gives the inquirer the admission criteria, rates, refund policy and a copy of the admission agreement, and answers questions.

The Administrator schedules a pre-admission interview with the prospective resident and, with the resident's consent, a family member or representative. The interview is at the facility or the resident's current location (22 CCR §87457).
With the resident's consent, the Administrator completes the pre-admission appraisal covering functional ability, mental condition and social needs, and records it in the resident file.

The Administrator screens the appraisal against the prohibited conditions list (22 CCR §87615), the facility's acceptance and retention limits and its staffing. If the resident has or needs services for a prohibited condition, the Administrator declines admission and refers the family to community resources. The reason is documented.

The Administrator checks compatibility with current residents (needs, behaviors, room assignment) using only factors that do not violate 22 CCR §87468.1(b). Decisions about room sharing and restroom assignment are made without regard to sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression or HIV status.
The Administrator requests the physician's report with physical examination and TB test/clearance. Admission does not take place until the physician's report is received and reviewed.
If the appraisal shows a hearing or other disability, the Administrator completes LIC 9158 and files it with the admission agreement (22 CCR §87507).
The Administrator makes the suitability decision and records the date, the decision and the reasons. If the resident is accepted, the Administrator sets the admission date.

Before or at admission, the Administrator reviews the admission agreement with the resident and representative: services, additional services, rates, payment, 60 days' written notice of rate changes, refunds, visiting and firearms policies, grievance procedure, grounds for eviction and the right to contact CDSS and the ombudsman. The agreement contains no liability-waiver provisions (22 CCR §87507).
The resident and the Licensee or Administrator sign and date the agreement within 7 days of admission. A copy is given immediately and a copy or notice of its availability is posted (22 CCR §87507).

At admission, the Administrator gives the resident and representative a written statement of personal rights (22 CCR §87468.1), explains it, and states that the resident's rights will not be violated. The resident signs an acknowledgement.

The Administrator records emergency information: emergency contacts, physician, preferred hospital, medications, allergies, advance directive status and responsible person. It is kept in the resident file and available in an emergency.
The Administrator explains the sign-in/sign-out procedure, stating that it is used only for safety and that the resident may leave at any time.
The Administrator requests the immunization record and records it in the file. The resident's decision to accept or decline vaccines is documented.
Within the time set in AD-02, the Administrator and resident develop the needs and services plan from the appraisal.
The Administrator reviews this admission policy every year and whenever the law changes (GOV-03).

responsibilities.duty: Approves admission criteria. Does not allow admissions outside the license or staffing capability.
Conducts the appraisal and suitability decision, ensures documents and agreements are complete, and informs the resident of rights.
Provides the physical examination, TB clearance and medical assessment.
Follow the sign-out procedure, use emergency information and respect the resident's personal rights.

documentation: Inquiry and pre-admission interview record
Pre-admission appraisal and suitability determination with reasons
Physician's report, physical examination and TB clearance
Signed admission agreement (and LIC 9158 if applicable)
Signed personal rights acknowledgement
Emergency information record
Immunization record or documented declination
Sign-in/sign-out log
Needs and services plan
Record of declined admissions and reasons

policies.category: Section B - Supportive Documents (B1, B2, B4-B17 for RCFE; B3 and B18 do not apply)
policies.title: Control of Property, Water Analysis and Insurance Information
policies.applies_to: Licensee, Administrator, maintenance staff
policies.purpose: To document that [AGENCY NAME] controls the property and may lawfully use it as an RCFE, that its water is safe, and that it carries the required insurance, with each document submitted with the application and kept current.
policies.policy:
[AGENCY NAME] will submit proof of control of the facility property, a water-safety analysis where the water source is private, and insurance information with its application (LIC 281 B11-B13). The facility will be maintained in accordance with 22 CCR §87303, including heat of at least 68°F and hot water between 105 and 120°F.

This policy meets LIC 281 item B11.1 (Control of Property, name and address of owner). The owner of the property is [PROPERTY OWNER NAME], [OWNER ADDRESS], and the facility address is [ADDRESS].

This policy meets LIC 281 item B11.2 (lease or rental agreement). If the licensee does not own the property, a copy of the lease or rental agreement, of any length, is submitted. The agreement must allow use as a licensed facility. If it precludes use as a facility, or operating the facility would be contrary to its terms, the license must be denied or withdrawn. The Licensee therefore confirms that the lease contains no such restriction.

This policy meets LIC 281 item B11.3 (proof of ownership). If the applicant owns the property, a property tax bill, deed or other document showing the facility's street address is submitted.

This policy meets LIC 281 item B12 (Bacterial Analysis of Water). [WATER SOURCE: public water utility / well or other private source]. This item applies only to a well or other private source. If the facility uses a public water utility, the application states that B12 does not apply. If the source is private, the application includes evidence of an on-site inspection of the source and a bacteriological analysis from a local or state health department or other qualified laboratory showing that the water is safe, signed by a qualified agency representative. This is required at initial licensure regardless of capacity. For a facility with capacity of 7 to 15, the water is tested every year (22 CCR §87303).

This policy meets LIC 281 item B13 (Insurance Information, RCFE only). [AGENCY NAME] states in the application whether it is insured, the type of coverage and the carrier. Liability insurance is carried at $1,000,000 per occurrence and $3,000,000 aggregate for injury to residents and guests caused by negligence (HSC §1569.605). Workers' compensation insurance will be in place once the facility has employees.

definitions.definition: The legal right to use the facility location, shown by ownership or by a lease or rental agreement.
A laboratory test showing a water supply is free of harmful bacteria.
A well or other water supply not provided by a public utility.
The most an insurer will pay in total for all claims during the policy period.

procedures: The Licensee identifies the legal owner of the property and records the owner's name and address on the application (B11.1).

If the Licensee leases the property, the Licensee obtains a signed copy of the lease or rental agreement. The Licensee reads it to confirm that operating an RCFE is permitted and that nothing in it precludes use as a facility (B11.2).

If the lease prohibits the use, the Licensee negotiates a written amendment or owner consent before applying and attaches it. The Licensee does not submit an application on a lease that bars use as a facility.

If the Licensee owns the property, the Licensee submits a current property tax bill, deed or similar document that shows the facility's street address (B11.3). The Licensee checks that the address matches the application.
The Administrator determines the water source. If the facility is on a public water utility, a utility bill is kept in the file and B12 is marked 'not applicable - public water.'

If the source is a well or other private source, the Licensee arranges an on-site inspection of the source by the local or state health department or a qualified laboratory, and orders the bacteriological test (B12).

The Licensee checks that the analysis is signed by a qualified agency representative and shows the water is safe. If the test fails, the Licensee corrects the problem (for example by disinfecting the well), retests and does not apply or admit residents until the water passes.
For capacity of 7 to 15, the Administrator schedules a water test every year (22 CCR §87303), diarizes the due date and files each result.

The Maintenance person checks monthly that heat is at least 68°F and hot water at taps used by residents is 105-120°F. The checks are logged and any out-of-range reading is reported to the Administrator the same day (22 CCR §87303).

The Licensee contacts an insurance broker for liability coverage of at least $1,000,000 per occurrence and $3,000,000 aggregate for injury to residents and guests caused by negligence (HSC §1569.605), and obtains a certificate of insurance.

The Licensee prepares the B13 statement: that the facility is insured, the type of coverage, and the carrier's name. If the facility is not yet insured, the statement says so. Coverage must be in place before residents are admitted.
Once the facility has employees, the Licensee obtains workers' compensation insurance and files the certificate.
The Administrator renews insurance before the expiration date, files updated certificates and tells the Licensee if any coverage lapses.
The Licensee uses the FC-01 checklist before submission to confirm that B11 through B13 documents are complete and consistent.
The Administrator reviews property, water and insurance records annually (GOV-03) and updates them after any change of owner, lease, water source or carrier.

responsibilities.duty: Secures lawful control of the property, purchases required insurance and ensures documents are submitted and kept current.
Keeps property, water and insurance records, schedules water testing and checks that heat and hot water meet standards.
Logs heat and hot water temperatures and reports problems.
Provide certificates of coverage and signed water analysis.

documentation: Property owner name and address record
Lease or rental agreement (and owner consent or amendment if needed)
Deed, property tax bill or other proof of ownership showing street address
Water source determination (public utility bill or private source documents)
On-site source inspection and signed bacteriological analysis; annual retests for capacity 7-15
Heat and hot water temperature log
Insurance statement (B13), liability certificate ($1M / $3M) and workers' compensation certificate

policies.category: Section B - Supportive Documents (B1, B2, B4-B17 for RCFE; B3 and B18 do not apply)
policies.title: Neighborhood Complaint Policy
policies.applies_to: All [AGENCY NAME] Residential Care Facility for the Elderly (RCFE) locations, all staff, the licensee, the administrator and any designee who meets with neighbors
policies.purpose: To give neighbors a clear, dependable way to raise concerns about the facility, to make sure [AGENCY NAME] responds to incidents and complaints immediately, and to keep a record showing every complaint was heard and resolved.
policies.policy:
This policy meets LIC 281 item B15 — Neighborhood Complaint Policy, which requires procedures for immediate response to incidents and complaints and a time when the owner, licensee or designee will be available to meet with neighborhood residents. The LIC 281 text applies B15 to non-resident-owner community care facilities serving six or fewer persons, but the LIC 281 Section B table marks it 'Required' in the RCFE column (LIC 281, Section B table p.10; B15 p.20). [AGENCY NAME] therefore adopts it for every RCFE it operates, whatever the size or ownership arrangement. The policy is part of the written plan of operation (22 CCR §87208).

(1) Immediate response: every neighborhood complaint or incident report is acknowledged the same day it is received, and the situation is addressed right away if it is still happening. (2) Meeting time: the owner, licensee or designee is available to meet with neighborhood residents every [MEETING DAY] from [START TIME] to [END TIME] at the facility, and at another mutually agreeable time within 3 business days of any request. (3) Published contact: the neighbor contact number, [NEIGHBOR CONTACT PHONE], is answered or returned the same day and is given to adjoining neighbors in writing. (4) Complaint log: every complaint is recorded with the date, complainant, response and resolution. Neighbors may raise concerns without fear of retaliation or of any effect on the care residents receive.

definitions.definition: Any person who lives, works or owns property near the facility, including adjoining and across-the-street households and businesses.
A person the licensee has named in writing to receive neighbor complaints and meet with neighbors, normally the administrator or the qualified substitute.
Same-day acknowledgment of the complaint and prompt action to stop or reduce any ongoing problem, such as noise, parking obstruction, odors or an incident outside the building.
The written record of each neighborhood complaint, how it was handled and how it was resolved.

procedures: Before opening, the administrator sets the standing neighbor meeting day and time ([MEETING DAY], [START TIME] to [END TIME]) and enters them in this policy.

Before opening, the administrator establishes the neighbor contact number ([NEIGHBOR CONTACT PHONE]) and names the person who answers it. A designee is named in writing if it is not the administrator.

Before opening, the administrator delivers a written notice to the adjoining and nearby neighbors. It gives the facility name and address, the contact number, the meeting day and time, and a short description of the facility. A copy of the notice is kept in the neighborhood complaint file.
The notice is redelivered to neighbors when the contact person, number or meeting time changes, and to new neighbors the administrator learns of.

Any staff member who receives a complaint in person, by phone or in writing takes the complainant's name, address, phone number and a description of the concern, and gives the information to the administrator or designee within the same shift. Staff never argue with or dismiss a neighbor.

The administrator or designee contacts the complainant the same day to acknowledge the concern. If the situation is ongoing (for example, noise, a blocked driveway or a resident outside the building), staff correct it immediately.

If the complaint involves a resident's safety, a possible injury, an unexplained absence, or suspected abuse or neglect, staff first protect the resident and then follow SP-02 (Incident and Accident Reporting), SP-03 (Elopement and Missing Resident), SP-01 (Abuse, Neglect and Exploitation Prevention and Reporting) and REC-02 (Required Reports to the State). Neighbor contact is handled after safety needs are met.

The administrator or designee records the complaint in the complaint log: date and time received, complainant name and contact information, nature of the complaint, who received it, and what was done at once.
The administrator or designee offers to meet the complainant at the next standing meeting time, or sooner by appointment, and meets in person if the neighbor wishes.

Within 7 calendar days, the administrator or designee investigates the concern, decides on corrective action, and tells the complainant the outcome by phone or in writing. If more time is needed, the complainant is told why and given a date.
The administrator records the response and resolution in the log, including the date the complainant was told and whether the complainant was satisfied.

Corrective actions that change operations (for example, delivery times, staff parking, outdoor activity hours or smoking areas) are communicated to all staff at the next staff meeting and written into the relevant policy or post orders.

Complaints that are not resolved within 30 days are reviewed by the licensee, who decides on further steps. A neighbor who remains dissatisfied is told they may contact the CDSS Adult and Senior Care Program at (916) 657-2592.

The administrator reviews the complaint log at least quarterly for patterns, and reports trends to the licensee and in the quality assurance review under GOV-03 (Policy Review, Document Control and Quality Assurance).
Complaint logs and related correspondence are kept at the facility and available to the licensing agency on request.

responsibilities.duty: Approves this policy, ensures the meeting time and contact number are honored, and reviews unresolved complaints.
Serves as the primary neighbor contact, holds the standing meeting, maintains the log and delivers the neighbor notice.
Acts for the administrator when named in writing and follows the same response times.
Receive neighbor concerns courteously, take the details and pass them to the administrator or designee within the same shift.

documentation: Neighborhood complaint log (date, complainant, response, resolution)
Copy of the written neighbor notice with the contact number and meeting time, and the dates it was delivered
Notes or summaries of neighbor meetings
Written designee appointment, if applicable
Quarterly complaint trend review

policies.category: Final checklist ('Have you remembered the following')
policies.title: Application Packet Final Checklist and Submission Review
policies.applies_to: Licensee, applicants, administrator and any staff or consultant who prepares or submits the RCFE license application packet for [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To make sure the complete RCFE license application packet is reviewed against the LIC 281 final checklist before submission, so nothing is missing, unsigned or inconsistent, and to manage the follow-up with the licensing analyst.
policies.policy:
[AGENCY NAME] completes a documented final review of the application packet against the 'Have you remembered the following' checklist on page 21 of LIC 281 (Application Instructions for a Facility License) before it is submitted to the CDSS Adult and Senior Care Program Centralized Applications Bureau. The packet is not mailed or uploaded until every item below is verified and initialed by a second person.

This policy meets the following LIC 281 final checklist items:
- Checklist-1 — Orientation: the applicant has attended an orientation for the facility type, and a copy of the orientation certificate(s) is enclosed.
- Checklist-2 — LIC 200: the application is signed and dated by all applicants.
- Checklist-3 — Emergency Disaster Plan (LIC 610E): a complete plan is enclosed that contains the elements required by 22 CCR §87212, including administrative authority and staff assignments, the fire safety plan, means of exiting, the assembly site, transportation, relocation sites, supervision and contact during relocation, contact with fire, law enforcement and disaster agencies, and notice to a resident's hospice agency.
- Checklist-4 — Facility Sketch (LIC 999): the sketch shows indoor and outdoor space and all exits, and is consistent with the plan of operation (22 CCR §87208).
- Checklist-5 — Financial information: all financial forms (LIC 401, 401a, 403, 403a and 404) are complete.
- Checklist-6 — Application fee: the application fee check is enclosed ($990 for 4-6 beds; $1,486.80 for 7-15 beds, per HSC §1569.185 and current CDSS instructions).
- Checklist-7 — Completeness and signatures: all necessary information is complete, and every form carries an original signature and a date.

definitions.definition: The CDSS Application Instructions for a Facility License, whose Sections A and B list the forms and supportive documents and whose final checklist is page 21.
The CDSS ASCP unit that receives and processes new RCFE license applications. Phone (833) 827-6084; email CCLASCPCAB@dss.ca.gov.
A written request from the licensing analyst for missing or corrected information.
A handwritten (wet) signature in ink, or another signature method that CDSS accepts at the time of submission.

procedures: The licensee names a packet coordinator in writing, normally the administrator or a designated applicant, who is responsible for the final review.

Two weeks before the planned submission date, the coordinator opens the current LIC 281 and prepares a packet tracking sheet that lists every Section A form and Section B supportive document, each with an owner and a due date.

Checklist-1: the coordinator confirms that each person who must attend orientation for the RCFE facility type has attended, and that the orientation certificate(s) are in the packet. The names on the certificates are compared against the names on the LIC 200.

Checklist-2: the coordinator confirms that the LIC 200 is complete and signed and dated in ink by every applicant (each owner, partner, officer or member listed). Missing signatures are collected before anything else proceeds.

Checklist-3: the coordinator checks the Emergency Disaster Plan (LIC 610E) against the elements in 22 CCR §87212, confirms that the plan is written and specific to the facility, and confirms that exit plans and telephone numbers are ready to be posted.

Checklist-4: the coordinator checks the Facility Sketch (LIC 999) for indoor and outdoor space, every room, and every exit. Dimensions, room uses and exits are cross-checked against the Emergency Disaster Plan and the plan of operation.

Checklist-5: the coordinator confirms that LIC 401, 401a, 403, 403a and 404 are complete, signed and dated, and that figures are consistent across forms (see SA-03). Supporting statements for start-up funds are attached.

Checklist-6: the coordinator prepares the application fee check for the correct amount for the licensed capacity (4-6 beds or 7-15 beds), confirms the payee against current CDSS instructions, and records the check number. A copy of the check is kept.

The coordinator confirms that the Section B documents required for RCFE (B1, B2 and B4-B17) are enclosed, including the theft and loss policy (B14), the neighborhood complaint policy (B15), the sample menu (B10) and the job descriptions and personnel policies (B4-B5). Items B3 and B18 do not apply to RCFE.

Checklist-7: the coordinator reads every page for blank fields, missing dates, missing original signatures and conflicting names, addresses or capacity numbers. Each form is checked once by the coordinator and once by a second reviewer, and both initial the tracking sheet.
The licensee reviews the packet and signs the tracking sheet to approve submission. The packet is not sent until the licensee has signed.
The coordinator makes a complete copy of the entire packet, including signature pages and the check, and files it in the permanent licensing file.
The coordinator submits the packet to the CDSS Centralized Applications Bureau as instructed in LIC 281, by a method that gives proof of delivery, and records the date and tracking information.
[AGENCY NAME] plans for a total processing time of about 90 to 120 days and does not accept residents, advertise a start date or sign admission agreements until the license is issued.

The coordinator checks the application status weekly. Any deficiency request from the analyst is logged the day it is received and answered within 5 business days, with the response copied to the licensing file.

After the license is issued, the coordinator moves the packet to the permanent facility file and hands off ongoing compliance tasks, including the annual fee due on each license anniversary (HSC §1569.185), to the administrator under GOV-02.

responsibilities.duty: Sign and date all forms, attend orientation, approve the packet for submission and ensure the fee is paid.
Runs the final review, keeps the tracking sheet, submits the packet and manages analyst deficiency requests.
Independently checks each checklist item and initials the tracking sheet.
Confirms that the plan of operation, disaster plan and sketch describe how the facility will actually operate.

documentation: Signed final checklist and packet tracking sheet with reviewer initials
Orientation certificate(s)
Complete copy of the submitted packet, including original-signature pages
Copy of the application fee check and proof of delivery
Deficiency request and response log

policies.title: Organization, Governing Body and Administrator Responsibilities
policies.applies_to: Licensee, governing body, administrator, designated qualified substitute and all department leads of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To define who is accountable for the operation of the RCFE, the qualifications and duties of the administrator, the use of a qualified substitute, and the changes that must be reported to the licensing agency.
policies.policy:
The licensee and governing body of [AGENCY NAME] are accountable for the operation of the facility and for its compliance with Title 22 and the RCFE Act. The governing body delegates day-to-day management to a certified administrator and holds the administrator to the standards below.

The administrator must be at least 21 years old, hold a high school diploma or equivalent, be of good character, and be certified as an RCFE administrator. For facilities of 16 or more beds, the added education and experience requirements apply (22 CCR §87405). The administrator is on the premises a sufficient number of hours to manage the facility. When the administrator is absent, a designated, qualified substitute is in charge and is named in the posted schedule.

[AGENCY NAME] keeps a written plan of operation current, including the administrative organization (22 CCR §87208). It notifies CDSS within 30 days of a new administrator and within 15 working days of a change of chief corporate officer (22 CCR §87211).

definitions.definition: The person, partnership, corporation, LLC or other legal entity to which the RCFE license is issued.
The owners, board, partners or managers who hold the licensee's authority and set the policy for the facility.
The certified individual responsible for the day-to-day operation of the facility and for compliance with licensing requirements.
A person who meets the qualifications required to act for the administrator and who is designated in writing to be in charge during the administrator's absence.
The highest-ranking officer or manager of a corporate or entity licensee, whose change must be reported to CDSS.

procedures: The governing body adopts an organization chart that shows the licensee, the governing body, the administrator, the qualified substitute, and the department leads (care, dietary, maintenance and housekeeping). The chart is kept in the plan of operation and updated whenever roles change.
The governing body names the administrator by written appointment, and the administrator accepts it in writing. The appointment records the administrator's certificate number and date of issue.

Before appointment, the licensee verifies that the administrator is at least 21, holds a high school diploma or equivalent, is of good character (with background clearance on file, see ST-02), and holds a current administrator certificate. For a facility of 16 or more beds, the licensee also verifies the added education and experience. See SB-02 for the verification file.

The governing body sets the administrator's scheduled on-premises hours in writing. The hours are set high enough to supervise care, staff, medications, records and the physical plant. The weekly schedule is posted where staff can see it.

The administrator names a qualified substitute in writing and confirms that the substitute meets the qualifications. The substitute's name and contact number are posted, and every staff member knows who is in charge on each shift.
Whenever the administrator is absent, the administrator briefs the substitute on residents with changes in condition, pending reports, medication concerns and any maintenance problems.

The administrator is responsible for staffing, training, admissions, appraisals and needs and services plans, resident rights, medication and records systems, building safety, and corrective action after any incident or inspection finding.

The administrator meets with the governing body at least monthly and reports on census, staffing, incidents, grievances, financial condition, survey findings and compliance, and the minutes record any decisions and assigned actions.
The governing body reviews and approves policy changes, the plan of operation, the annual budget and any capacity changes. See GOV-03 for annual policy review.

When an administrator leaves, the licensee appoints a replacement who meets all requirements. Within 30 days of a new administrator, the licensee notifies CDSS in writing (22 CCR §87211) and files the notice and the new administrator's certification information in the licensing file.
When the chief corporate officer changes, the licensee notifies CDSS within 15 working days (22 CCR §87211). The notice is signed, copied and tracked to confirmation.

If the facility receives a foreclosure notice, unlawful detainer, bankruptcy filing, rent default notice or utility shut-off notice, the licensee provides written notice to CDSS within 2 business days, as required by 22 CCR §87211. The governing body understands that a civil penalty of $100 per day, up to $2,000, applies to late notice, and that applicants must be told before they sign an admission agreement.

The administrator keeps the plan of operation current. When services, staffing, the sketch, transportation, resident money handling, the visiting policy or the infection control plan changes, the administrator updates the plan (22 CCR §87208) and submits any change that requires CDSS approval or notification.

The administrator completes continuing education to maintain certification (40 hours every 2 years) and keeps the certificates on file. The licensee verifies this at renewal and at each annual evaluation.

The governing body evaluates the administrator in writing at least once a year against these duties, the results of internal reviews, and licensing findings. The evaluation is signed by both parties and filed.

responsibilities.duty: Holds ultimate accountability, appoints and evaluates the administrator, approves policy and finances, and makes required notifications to CDSS.
Manages daily operations and compliance, is on premises sufficient hours, supervises staff and reports to the governing body.
Acts in charge during the administrator's absence with the same responsibility for resident safety and compliance.
Carry out the plan of operation in their areas and report problems to the administrator promptly.

documentation: Organization chart and plan of operation
Administrator appointment letter, certificate and continuing education records
Posted administrator schedule and substitute designation
Governing body meeting minutes
Copies of notices to CDSS (new administrator, change of chief corporate officer, financial notices)
Annual administrator evaluation

policies.title: Licensure, Posting and Regulatory Compliance
policies.applies_to: Licensee, administrator, qualified substitute and maintenance staff of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To keep the facility licensed and in good standing by posting required documents, paying fees on time, obtaining fire clearance, meeting physical plant standards, and notifying CDSS before capacity or location changes.
policies.policy:
[AGENCY NAME] operates only within the terms of its RCFE license and keeps every required document, fee and clearance current.

Posting: the license, resident rights, emergency exit plans and emergency telephone numbers (22 CCR §87212), and the Ombudsman CRISISline 1-800-231-4024 with the local ombudsman number are posted where residents, visitors and staff can see them.

Fees: the annual license fee is paid by each license anniversary: $495.60 for 4-6 beds or $742.80 for 7-15 beds. Late payment adds a 50 percent late fee. A capacity change fee of $25 applies (HSC §1569.185).

Changes: CDSS is notified before capacity is changed ($25) or before the facility relocates (a fee of 50 percent of the application fee).

Fire clearance: a fire clearance is required before licensure. A separate fire clearance is required before the facility accepts or keeps nonambulatory or bedridden residents (22 CCR §87202).

Physical plant: no more than 2 residents per bedroom, with at least 1 toilet and washbasin per 6 persons and 1 tub or shower per 10, counting live-in staff and family (22 CCR §87307). Heat is at least 68°F, hot water is 105 to 120°F, the plant is maintained, and private water supplies are tested annually for facilities with a capacity of 7 to 15 (22 CCR §87303).

definitions.definition: The yearly date on which the annual fee for the license is due.
Written approval from the local fire authority or State Fire Marshal that the facility meets fire safety requirements for the intended residents.
A resident who is unable to leave a building unassisted under emergency conditions, including a resident who is bedridden or who needs a wheelchair or other mobility device to exit.
The maximum number of residents the license allows.

procedures: The administrator posts the original license in a prominent location. The location is recorded on the monthly environmental checklist.

The administrator posts the statement of resident rights, emergency exit plans and emergency telephone numbers (fire, law enforcement, poison control, disaster agencies, the licensing agency and the administrator), and the Ombudsman CRISISline 1-800-231-4024 with the local ombudsman number. The postings are checked monthly and replaced if damaged or out of date.

The administrator calendars the license anniversary date and the annual fee ($495.60 for 4-6 beds or $742.80 for 7-15 beds). Payment is requested 30 days before the due date and made at least 10 days before it, and the payment confirmation is filed. A late payment is escalated to the licensee at once because of the 50 percent late fee.

Before any capacity increase or decrease, the licensee submits the request to CDSS with the $25 capacity change fee and waits for written approval. No additional resident is admitted before approval and any needed fire clearance.

Before any relocation, the licensee contacts the CDSS Adult and Senior Care Program at (916) 657-2592, submits the required application, and pays the relocation fee of 50 percent of the application fee. The facility does not move residents to a new site before the license for that site is issued.
Before licensure, the licensee obtains the fire clearance from the local fire authority. A copy is kept at the facility.

Before admitting or keeping any nonambulatory or bedridden resident, the administrator confirms that the facility holds a separate fire clearance for that use (22 CCR §87202). Without it, no such resident is admitted, and a current resident who becomes nonambulatory or bedridden is handled under AD-03 and AD-04.

The administrator checks the building monthly against the physical plant standards: no more than 2 residents per bedroom, toilets and washbasins at 1 per 6 persons and tubs or showers at 1 per 10 (counting live-in staff and family), heat of at least 68°F, and hot water at 105 to 120°F measured at resident-use fixtures. Results are logged.
If the facility has a private water supply and a capacity of 7 to 15, the administrator has the water tested annually by a qualified laboratory and files the results (see SB-07).
The administrator reviews the emergency exit plans and phone numbers each quarter and whenever a number or exit changes, and updates the Emergency Disaster Plan under SP-05.
The administrator keeps current copies of Title 22 regulations, the RCFE Act and licensing notices, and shares changes with staff at the next staff meeting.
During any CDSS visit or inspection, the administrator or qualified substitute cooperates fully, gives the evaluator access to the facility, residents and records, and keeps notes of the findings.
Any deficiency is answered by the plan of correction deadline given in writing. The administrator documents the correction and the date completed, and reports the result to the licensee.
Incidents and events that must be reported to CDSS are handled under REC-02 (Required Reports to the State), and the administrator confirms the report dates are met.
The licensee reviews this policy's compliance calendar (fees, fire clearance, water test, posting checks) each quarter as part of GOV-03.

responsibilities.duty: Pays fees, requests capacity or location changes, obtains fire clearances and ensures the facility operates within its license.
Maintains postings, the compliance calendar and the physical plant checks, and answers inspections.
Measure heat and hot water temperatures, correct plant problems and keep logs.
Cooperates with inspectors and keeps postings and checks current when the administrator is absent.

documentation: Posted license, resident rights notice, exit plans, phone numbers and Ombudsman CRISISline notice
Annual fee payment receipts
Capacity change and relocation correspondence with CDSS
Fire clearance(s), including any clearance for nonambulatory or bedridden residents
Monthly physical plant and temperature logs
Water test results, if applicable
Inspection reports and plans of correction

policies.title: Policy Review, Document Control and Quality Assurance
policies.applies_to: Licensee, administrator, infection control lead, department leads and all staff of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To keep policies accurate and current, to ensure staff know and follow them, and to catch compliance problems through internal reviews and trend analysis before a surveyor does.
policies.policy:
[AGENCY NAME] reviews every policy in this manual at least annually, as a facility standard. The infection control plan (LIC 9282) is also reviewed annually, after an outbreak declaration, and whenever the licensing agency asks (22 CCR §87470). The plan of operation is kept current as changes occur (22 CCR §87208).

The administrator runs quarterly internal mock inspections of medication records, personnel files (training, health screening and clearances), appraisals and admission agreements. Incident, injury and grievance reports are trended, and corrective actions are recorded. Reports that must be made to the licensing agency, and the timelines for them, are tracked against 22 CCR §87211 (see REC-02).

Every policy shows an effective date and a revision history, and a signed staff acknowledgment is kept for each version.

definitions.definition: The system that assigns each policy an effective date, version number and revision history, and ensures only the current version is in use.
An internal review that uses the licensing evaluator's approach to check records and practices.
A specific step, with an owner and a due date, taken to fix a problem found in a review or trend.
The staff member named in the infection control plan and trained by a qualified professional to lead infection prevention.

procedures: The administrator keeps a policy master list showing each policy ID, title, version, effective date, last review date and next review date. The list is kept in the policy binder and in the electronic file.
Each policy carries an effective date, version number and revision history table. Superseded versions are marked 'Superseded', dated, and kept for 3 years in an archive file.

At least annually, the administrator and the relevant department lead review each policy against current Title 22 regulations, CDSS notices, incidents and survey findings. The reviewer signs and dates the policy review page, whether or not changes are made.
The governing body approves changes. Approved revisions are issued with a new version number and effective date, and old copies are removed from the binder and work areas.
Within 14 days of a revision, each affected employee reads the changed policy and signs the acknowledgment. The administrator trains staff on significant changes at a staff meeting.
New employees read and sign the acknowledgment for the policy manual during orientation (see ST-03).

The Infection Control Lead and administrator review the infection control plan (LIC 9282) annually, after any outbreak declaration, and when the licensing agency asks. The review is documented and any plan changes are shared with staff. The Infection Control Lead's training by a qualified professional is verified at each review (see SP-07).

Each quarter the administrator or a designated reviewer who is not responsible for the records being reviewed performs a mock inspection. The review covers a sample of medication administration and assistance records, personnel files (training hours, health screening and TB results, background clearances), resident appraisals and needs and services plans, and signed admission agreements.
The reviewer uses a written checklist and records each finding. A finding is any missing, late, unsigned or inconsistent item.
Each finding is assigned a corrective action, an owner and a due date, usually within 30 days. The administrator tracks open items on a log and verifies completion by re-checking the records.

Monthly, the administrator compiles incident and accident reports, falls, injuries, medication errors, grievances and complaints by type, location, time of day, shift and resident. The administrator looks for patterns and reports them to the governing body.

The administrator checks that reportable events were reported to the licensing agency within the timelines of 22 CCR §87211 (for example, 7 days for a written report of a death or serious injury, 24 hours for an outbreak, and the next working day for a fire), and records any late report and the reason.

When a trend is found (for example, repeated falls on night shift), the administrator starts an action plan, such as a change in staffing, environment, training or the resident's needs and services plan, and re-checks the data after 60 days.

The administrator presents a quality assurance summary, with the mock inspection findings, trend data, open corrective actions and policy review status, to the governing body each quarter. The minutes record decisions.

Results of mock inspections and quality reviews are kept for at least 3 years and are available to the licensing agency on request. Resident confidentiality is protected in all review documents (see RR-06).

responsibilities.duty: Approves policies and revisions and reviews quarterly quality assurance reports.
Maintains document control, assigns and tracks reviews, runs or assigns mock inspections and closes corrective actions.
Leads the annual and event-triggered review of the infection control plan.
Review policies for their areas, correct findings and report trends.
Read and acknowledge policies and follow the current version.

documentation: Policy master list and revision histories
Signed staff acknowledgments by policy version
Annual policy review sign-off pages
Infection control plan review record
Quarterly mock inspection checklists, findings and corrective action log
Monthly incident, injury and grievance trend reports
Quarterly quality assurance summaries and governing body minutes

policies.title: Corporate Compliance, Fraud and Billing Integrity (including Assisted Living Waiver)
policies.applies_to: Licensee, governing body, administrator, billing and admissions staff and all employees and contractors of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] is honest in every statement and bill it makes to residents, payers and regulators, and to set out the added requirements that apply if it enrolls in the Medi-Cal Assisted Living Waiver (ALW).
policies.policy:
[AGENCY NAME] does not make false claims or statements to the licensing agency or to any payer, and does not bill for services it did not provide. Every report, application, fee payment (including annual fees under HSC §1569.185), invoice and record is accurate and complete.

The following applies only if [AGENCY NAME] enrolls in the Medi-Cal Assisted Living Waiver. The facility follows the DHCS provider agreement and the tier rates (T2031 daily rates currently range from Tier 1, $95.69, to Tier 5, $270.80). The waiver does not pay room and board. The resident pays it, typically at the SSI/SSP board-and-care basic services rate of $1,444.07 per month in 2026, from a $1,626.07 grant, with $182 kept by the resident for personal needs. The HCBS settings rule (42 CFR §441.301(c)) applies to ALW participants only and requires a lease or agreement, privacy, resident choice, and access to food and visitors.

The DHCS enrollment packet is notarized (DHCS 6204, 6207 and 6208) and carries a $750 CY2026 application fee. ALW providers need licensed nursing either on call or employed, and an Individual Response System if housing more than 6 participants.

definitions.definition: A bill, report or statement to a payer or regulator that is knowingly untrue or that overstates services, resident needs or amounts owed.
A Medi-Cal program run by DHCS that pays enrolled RCFEs a daily tier rate for assisted living services to eligible participants. It does not pay room and board.
The federal home and community-based services requirement at 42 CFR §441.301(c) for settings where waiver participants live.
An electronic system that lets a participant summon help; the ALW requires one if more than 6 participants are housed.
The person designated by the licensee to oversee this policy, receive reports of concerns and ensure follow-up.

procedures: The licensee designates a Compliance Officer, normally the administrator, or the licensee if the administrator's own conduct is at issue, and posts the person's name and contact number for staff.

At hire and annually, every employee is trained on this policy: what counts as a false statement or false claim, how to record services honestly, and how to report a concern. Attendance is documented.

Staff record only services actually provided, at the time they are provided. Altering, backdating or copying forward records to show services that did not occur is prohibited and grounds for discipline up to termination.

Reports, applications and statements to CDSS and other agencies are prepared from source records and reviewed by a second person before signing. Whoever signs is certifying that the content is true and complete.

Resident charges follow the signed admission agreement (see RR-03). The admissions staff member never bills an amount, fee or rate that is not in the agreement or in a properly given written notice of change.

Before the facility submits a bill to a resident, family or payer, the administrator or billing staff reconciles it to the agreement and to service and attendance records. Errors are corrected and any overpayment is refunded to the resident or payer within 30 days of discovery.
No staff member solicits or accepts payment, gifts or kickbacks in exchange for referrals, admissions or services. Offers are reported to the Compliance Officer.

If [AGENCY NAME] decides to apply to the ALW, the governing body approves it in writing. The administrator prepares the DHCS enrollment packet, including the notarized DHCS 6204, 6207 and 6208 and the $750 CY2026 application fee, and confirms the current requirements with DHCS before submitting.

Before enrolling, the administrator confirms the facility can meet the ALW staffing conditions: licensed nursing on call or employed, and an Individual Response System if housing more than 6 participants. If it cannot, it does not enroll.

For each ALW participant, the facility bills the DHCS tier rate only for the tier assigned and only for days of service delivered. Room and board is billed to the participant only, at an amount consistent with the agreement and the SSI/SSP basic rate, and never bills ALW for room and board.

Admission agreements for ALW participants meet the HCBS settings rule (42 CFR §441.301(c)): a lease or agreement, privacy, resident choice, and access to food and visitors. Practices that restrict these are changed or documented as an individualized, resident-supported exception under the applicable rules, with approval from the care team.

The Compliance Officer checks new hires and contractors against the applicable federal and state exclusion lists (for example, the OIG List of Excluded Individuals/Entities and the Medi-Cal Suspended and Ineligible Provider List) before hire and annually. Anyone listed is not hired and is removed from any role that touches billing or care.

Anyone who suspects fraud, a false claim, a billing error or a violation reports it to the Compliance Officer or the licensee, in person, in writing or anonymously. Reports about the Compliance Officer go directly to the licensee. Retaliation against anyone who reports in good faith is prohibited.

The Compliance Officer opens a file for each report, investigates within 14 days, interviews people involved, stops any improper practice, corrects and repays errors, and records the outcome and any discipline. Serious findings are reported to the governing body and, where required, to the appropriate agency.

Each quarter, the Compliance Officer audits a sample of invoices and service records against the agreement, and for ALW participants checks the tier and days billed. The results are included in the quality assurance report under GOV-03.

responsibilities.duty: Sets the expectation of honest conduct, designates the Compliance Officer, approves ALW enrollment and acts on serious findings.
Trains staff, receives and investigates reports, runs exclusion checks and audits billing.
Ensures accurate records, reports and billing and, if enrolled in the ALW, meets the provider agreement and HCBS requirements.
Bill only per the signed agreement and reconcile bills to services delivered.
Document honestly and report concerns without fear of retaliation.

documentation: Compliance Officer designation and posted contact information
Training attendance records
Exclusion screening results
Compliance report and investigation files
Quarterly billing audit results
If enrolled in the ALW: the DHCS provider agreement, notarized DHCS 6204/6207/6208, tier assignments, billing records and HCBS settings documentation

policies.title: Resident Rights and Responsibilities (Personal Rights and Discipline)
policies.applies_to: All residents and their representatives; all staff, volunteers and contractors of [AGENCY NAME] at [ADDRESS]
policies.purpose: To ensure every resident of [AGENCY NAME] is told of, and enjoys, the personal rights guaranteed to residents of California Residential Care Facilities for the Elderly, to prohibit corporal or unusual punishment, and to prohibit discrimination in the ways the regulation specifies.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] recognizes, posts and gives to every resident the personal rights listed in 22 CCR §87468.1 (18 rights). These include the right to be treated with dignity; to be free from punishment, humiliation, intimidation and abuse; to be told how to complain to CDSS Community Care Licensing and the Long-Term Care Ombudsman; to leave the facility at any time and not be locked in; to receive private visits from ombudsmen and advocates at reasonable hours without prior notice; to keep and spend one's own money; to use the telephone, send and receive mail, and vote; to refuse care; and to move out. The facility will not deny admission, or transfer, discharge, room-share, assign a room or restroom, refuse a resident's preferred name or pronouns, or restrict association, based on a resident's actual or perceived sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression or HIV status. These protections cannot be waived by the Department or by the facility. This policy meets LIC 281 item B8.1 — Rules of Discipline / Personal Rights (personal rights apply to all facility categories; the detailed discipline-policy content in LIC 281 B8 applies only to group homes and foster family agencies). This policy meets LIC 281 item B8.2 — Discipline policies: [AGENCY NAME] states clearly that no corporal or unusual punishment will be used on any resident, and that nothing in the facility's rules or practices violates a personal right. Staff are trained on personal rights as part of orientation and ongoing training. If [AGENCY NAME] enrolls in the Medi-Cal Assisted Living Waiver, residents in that program also receive the protections of the federal HCBS settings rule (42 CFR 441.301(c)), including privacy, choice, and access to food and visitors.

definitions.definition: The rights of residents listed in 22 CCR §87468.1, which the facility must post and give to each resident at admission.

Any physical punishment, or any humiliating, frightening, deprivation-based or otherwise unusual response to a resident's behavior. Examples are withholding food, visitors, mail, telephone, money or medical care, or confining a resident to a room.
A person's way of presenting gender through name, pronouns, clothing, appearance and behavior.
A person legally authorized to act for a resident, such as a conservator or agent under a power of attorney. Authority is verified before the person acts for a resident.
The federal Home and Community-Based Services standards at 42 CFR 441.301(c). They apply only to residents enrolled in the Medi-Cal Assisted Living Waiver.

procedures: The Administrator keeps the current, complete text of the personal rights in 22 CCR §87468.1 (all 18 rights) as the facility's Personal Rights notice. It is reviewed under GOV-03 at least annually and whenever the regulation changes.

Before or at admission, the Administrator or designee reads or explains the Personal Rights notice in the resident's language and in plain terms, and gives the resident (and representative, if any) a copy. If the resident has a hearing, vision or cognitive disability, the explanation is adapted (see RR-07).

The resident or representative signs and dates an acknowledgment that the rights were explained and a copy was given. The acknowledgment is filed in the resident record. A resident's refusal to sign is noted and dated by staff, and the resident still receives the notice.

The Personal Rights notice is posted in a prominent public area at [ADDRESS], at a height and in print size readable by residents. The notice includes how to contact CDSS Community Care Licensing (ASCP (916) 657-2592) and the Long-Term Care Ombudsman (CRISISline 1-800-231-4024).

Residents are never locked in the facility or in their rooms. Delayed-egress or secured-perimeter arrangements for dementia care follow HS-04, SP-03 and SP-04. No door arrangement may be used to prevent a competent resident from leaving.

Staff do not use or threaten corporal or unusual punishment, humiliation, intimidation, or the withholding of food, visitors, mail, phone, money, medication or care as a response to a resident's behavior. Behavioral concerns are handled by redirection, reassessment and the Needs and Services Plan (AD-02), and, if needed, by notice of discharge under AD-04 and not by punishment.

At admission, and when a resident's circumstances change, the Administrator or designee asks each resident for their preferred name and pronouns and records them. All staff use them in speech, signage and records.

Admission, transfer, discharge, room-sharing, and room and restroom assignments are decided only on the criteria in AD-01, AD-03 and AD-04. The Administrator reviews any proposed decision involving a resident who has disclosed sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression or HIV status to confirm that status is not a factor. The reviewer documents that confirmation.

Staff may not deny a resident the company of any person, including a partner or friend, because of the sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression or HIV status of the resident or the visitor. Visiting hours and rules are stated in the admission agreement (RR-03) and applied equally.
