Ombudsmen and advocates are admitted for private visits at reasonable hours without prior notice, as described in RR-02. Staff do not ask for advance notice or demand to be present.

Each resident controls their own money, mail, telephone use and voting, and may refuse care. Refusals that affect health are reported to the resident's physician and representative and recorded under HS-03. They are never punished.

All new staff receive personal-rights training in orientation before working with residents, and all staff receive refresher training at least annually under ST-03. Attendance is recorded in the personnel file (ST-05).

A resident or staff member who believes a right has been violated reports it to the Administrator or may complain directly to CDSS Community Care Licensing or the Ombudsman. The Administrator handles the report under RR-02. Suspected abuse is reported under SP-01 immediately.

If [AGENCY NAME] enrolls in the Assisted Living Waiver, the Administrator confirms that for waiver residents the setting provides a lease or agreement, privacy, resident choice, and access to food and visitors as required by 42 CFR 441.301(c). Any facility rule that would limit one of these must be revised.
No staff member may retaliate against a resident or staff member for asserting a personal right or making a complaint. Retaliation is grounds for discipline up to termination under ST-06.
The Administrator reviews personal-rights compliance quarterly (observations, resident feedback, grievance log) and records findings in the quality assurance file under GOV-03.

responsibilities.duty: Adopt this policy, ensure no facility rule conflicts with the personal rights, and ensure resources are available to meet them.
Maintain and post the notice, explain rights at admission, review admission, transfer and discharge decisions for discrimination, train staff and conduct the quarterly review.
Treat residents with dignity, use preferred names and pronouns, never use punishment, and report suspected rights violations at once.
Are encouraged to respect the rights and safety of other residents and to follow reasonable house rules that do not conflict with personal rights.

documentation: Personal Rights notice (posted copy and the version dated for the current review)
Signed acknowledgment of rights in each resident record
Preferred name and pronoun entry in each resident record
Personal-rights training attendance records
Documentation of the discrimination check on admission, transfer, discharge and room-assignment decisions
Quarterly rights-compliance review notes

policies.title: Grievances, Complaints and Ombudsman Access
policies.applies_to: All residents, representatives and families; all staff of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To give residents a clear and safe way to raise concerns, to make sure they know how to reach CDSS Community Care Licensing and the Long-Term Care Ombudsman, and to guarantee ombudsman and advocate access.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] has a written grievance procedure, which is included in each resident's admission agreement (22 CCR §87507). Residents are told, at admission and by posted notice, how to complain to CDSS Community Care Licensing and to the Long-Term Care Ombudsman (22 CCR §87468.1). Ombudsmen and advocates may visit residents privately at reasonable hours without prior notice. Every grievance, the response and the outcome are logged. No resident, family member or staff member is retaliated against for making a complaint. Allegations of abuse, neglect or exploitation are not handled as ordinary grievances. They are reported immediately as required by W&I Code §15630 and SP-01.

definitions.definition: Any oral or written complaint or concern from a resident, representative or family member about care, services, staff, other residents, charges, rights or the facility.
The Long-Term Care Ombudsman Program of the California Department of Aging, which advocates for residents of long-term care facilities. It can be reached at CRISISline 1-800-231-4024.
A person acting on a resident's behalf, such as a legal services or protection-and-advocacy representative, who is entitled to private visits at reasonable hours.
Any adverse action taken because a person made or supported a complaint, such as threats of discharge, reduced care, changed room assignment or hostile treatment.

procedures: The grievance procedure is written into each admission agreement in plain language (RR-03), and the Administrator reviews it with the resident or representative at signing, no later than 7 days after admission.

At admission the Administrator or designee gives each resident a Grievance and Complaint notice listing: the Administrator's name and number ([ADMINISTRATOR NAME], [PHONE]); CDSS Community Care Licensing ASCP (916) 657-2592 and the local licensing office [LOCAL CCL REGIONAL OFFICE PHONE]; and the Long-Term Care Ombudsman CRISISline 1-800-231-4024 and the local ombudsman [LOCAL OMBUDSMAN PHONE].
The same information is posted in a common area at [ADDRESS] in large print, with the Ombudsman and licensing numbers visible at all times.

Any staff member who receives a complaint, orally or in writing, accepts it respectfully, records the date, the person, the nature of the complaint and any immediate safety issue, and gives it to the Administrator the same day. Staff help residents who cannot write or who need language or disability accommodation (RR-07).

If the complaint alleges or suggests abuse, neglect or exploitation, the staff member does not wait for the grievance process. The staff member follows SP-01 and reports immediately by phone, with the written report to follow within the time the law requires (SOC 341).
The Administrator enters the complaint in the Grievance Log within one business day, and acknowledges it to the complainant, orally or in writing, within 2 business days.

The Administrator investigates promptly. This includes talking with the resident, involved staff and witnesses, and reviewing records. The Administrator takes immediate steps to protect the resident from any ongoing risk.

The Administrator gives the complainant a written or oral response, in a form the resident can understand, within 10 calendar days. The response explains what was found, what action was or will be taken, and that the resident may take the concern to CDSS Community Care Licensing or the Ombudsman at any time. If more time is needed, the Administrator explains why and sets a date.

The Administrator records the response, the outcome and the date in the Grievance Log, and asks the complainant whether the matter is resolved. An unresolved complaint is escalated to the governing body.

Residents may contact CDSS Community Care Licensing or the Ombudsman at any time, with or without first using the facility procedure. Staff do not discourage, delay or screen these contacts. Residents may use a private phone or be helped to make the call or send mail unopened.

Ombudsmen and advocates are admitted at reasonable hours without prior notice. Staff ask the visitor to sign in as the facility does for other visitors, but do not require an appointment, ask the reason for the visit or stay in the room. Private space is offered for the visit.

Staff do not tell residents they will be charged, moved or discharged because of a complaint. Any adverse action involving a resident or staff member who has complained within the prior 90 days is reviewed by the Administrator and, where the Administrator is involved, by the governing body.
The Administrator summarizes the Grievance Log quarterly (counts, themes, response times, open items) and uses the results in quality assurance under GOV-03.
Staff are trained on this policy at orientation and annually (ST-03). Training includes how to receive a complaint and the prohibition on retaliation.

responsibilities.duty: Receive, log, investigate and answer grievances, ensure postings are current, protect complainants from retaliation and report trends to the governing body.
Accept every complaint, pass it to the Administrator the same day, report suspected abuse under SP-01 and never retaliate.
Review escalated or unresolved grievances and the quarterly summary.
May raise concerns with staff, the Administrator, CDSS Community Care Licensing or the Ombudsman at any time.

documentation: Grievance Log (date received, complainant, nature, investigator, response date, outcome, resolution confirmation)
Written responses to complainants
Posted Grievance and Complaint notice with licensing and Ombudsman contact numbers
Signed acknowledgment of the notice in the resident record
Ombudsman and advocate visitor log entries
Quarterly grievance summary in the quality assurance file

policies.title: Admission Agreement, Fees, Deposits and Refunds
policies.applies_to: Administrator, admission staff, business office, residents and their representatives
policies.purpose: To make sure each resident receives a clear individual written admission agreement that meets California requirements, so residents and families understand services, charges, refunds, rights and the conditions of discharge before they move in.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] enters into an individual written admission agreement with each resident, as required by 22 CCR §87507. The agreement is in at least 12-point type and plain language, with titled sections. It is signed and dated by the resident or representative and the facility within 7 days of admission. The resident receives a copy immediately, and a copy or a notice of its availability is posted. The agreement states basic services, additional services (the optional or extra-charge services), rates and payment terms, refund conditions, preadmission fee limits and refunds, the visiting policy, the firearms policy, the grievance procedure, eviction grounds and notice rights, and the resident's right to contact CDSS and the Long-Term Care Ombudsman. Rates are changed only on 60 days' written notice. Form LIC 9158 is attached when the appraisal shows a hearing or other disability. The agreement contains no provision that waives or limits the facility's liability.

definitions.definition: The individual written contract between [AGENCY NAME] and the resident (or representative) setting out services, charges and the rights and duties of each party.
The services included in the base monthly rate, as listed in the agreement.
Services available for an extra charge, with each charge listed in the agreement.
Any fee or deposit collected before admission, which is limited and refundable as the agreement and regulation provide.
The state form for residents whose appraisal shows a hearing or other disability, attached to the agreement when required.

procedures: The Administrator maintains the facility's standard admission agreement. It is prepared in at least 12-point type, in plain language, with section titles, and is reviewed under GOV-03 at least annually and whenever rates, services or regulations change.

Before any agreement is signed, the Administrator or designee completes the pre-admission screening and appraisal (AD-01) and confirms that the resident's needs can be met (AD-03). The facility does not admit anyone whose needs it cannot serve, and does not rely on the agreement to cover this.

The Administrator or designee goes through the agreement section by section with the resident and representative, in their language. Accommodation for hearing, vision or cognitive limitations is provided (RR-07).

The agreement states each basic service included in the monthly rate, such as room, meals, housekeeping, laundry, supervision, medication assistance, activities and transportation as applicable. It lists each additional service with its price, and the payment terms, due date and accepted payment methods.

The agreement states the conditions under which refunds are made, and the limits on and refund of any preadmission fee. Refunds are issued within the time the agreement states. The business office records each deposit, refund and the date.

The agreement states that rates and fees may be changed only after at least 60 days' written notice. The Administrator sends each rate-change notice by hand delivery or mail, keeps a copy in the resident record, and does not apply an increase before the 60 days have passed.

The agreement states the facility's visiting policy and firearms policy. The visiting policy must be consistent with the personal rights in RR-01, including the right to private visits from ombudsmen and advocates without prior notice.
The agreement includes the facility's grievance procedure (RR-02) and the right to contact CDSS Community Care Licensing and the Ombudsman, with current telephone numbers.
The agreement includes the eviction grounds and the resident's notice rights, using the Department's required wording without modification. Procedures for relocation are in AD-04.
If the appraisal shows a hearing or other disability, the Administrator attaches LIC 9158 to the agreement and reviews it with the resident. A copy is filed with the agreement.

No clause may waive the resident's rights or release the facility from liability for its own acts. The Administrator removes any such wording before the form is used, and any modification of the standard agreement is reviewed by the governing body or its counsel.

The resident or representative and the Administrator sign and date the agreement no later than 7 days after admission. The resident receives a complete copy immediately after signing. The signed original is placed in the resident record (REC-01).
The Administrator posts a copy of the agreement, or a notice that copies are available on request, in a public area at [ADDRESS].
When a representative signs, the Administrator confirms the representative's authority and records the basis (for example, power of attorney or conservatorship) in the record.
When the agreement is amended (for example, when additional services are added), the amendment is in writing, explained to the resident, signed and dated, and a copy is given immediately.

If the facility enrolls in the Medi-Cal Assisted Living Waiver, the Administrator reviews the agreement for each waiver resident so that it does not conflict with waiver and HCBS settings requirements (GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Maintain the compliant agreement form, explain it to each resident, obtain signatures within 7 days, give copies, post notice and issue 60-day rate-change notices.
Record payments, deposits and refunds accurately and on time, and keep records of rate-change notices.
Approve rates and the agreement form and ensure no liability-waiver wording is used.
Review, ask questions about and sign the agreement, and pay charges as agreed.

documentation: Signed and dated admission agreement (original in the resident record; copy given to the resident)
LIC 9158, when applicable
Posted copy of the agreement or notice of availability
Preadmission fee and deposit receipts and refund records
60-day written rate-change notices with proof of delivery
Signed amendments to the agreement
Record of the representative's authority

policies.title: Resident Funds, Personal Property and Theft and Loss
policies.applies_to: Administrator, all staff, business office, residents and representatives
policies.purpose: To protect resident money and belongings, to preserve each resident's right to keep and spend their own money, and to provide the written Theft and Loss Policy required for the license application.
policies.policy: Residents have the right to keep and spend their own money (22 CCR §87468.1). [AGENCY NAME] [DOES NOT HOLD / HOLDS] resident cash; the Administrator records the decision here before licensure. If the facility holds resident cash, it files the Resident Cash Resources Affidavit (LIC 400) and surety bond (LIC 402), keeps receipts and accounting records, and maintains a separate account titled as the residents' money with no commingling with facility funds (22 CCR §87217). This policy meets LIC 281 item B14 — Theft and Loss Policy (RCFE only), and includes provisions for: (1) an inventory of personal property at admission; (2) modification of the inventory; (3) practices to safeguard personal property upon the death of the resident; (4) documentation and reporting of loss of personal property; (5) the method of marking personal property; and (6) the method for providing a secure area for safekeeping of resident personal property. The inventory is kept in the resident record, and the resident receives a copy.

definitions.definition: Items of a resident that the resident brings to or acquires at the facility, such as clothing, jewelry, eyeglasses, hearing aids, dentures, electronics, furniture, papers and keepsakes.
Money belonging to a resident that the facility holds or manages at the resident's request or authority.
Mixing resident funds with facility operating funds or with the funds of other residents. It is prohibited.
A dated, signed list of a resident's personal property with its description and condition.
A locked area, such as a locked cabinet, drawer or safe, with restricted staff access, used for property the resident wants the facility to safeguard.

procedures: Before licensure, the Administrator and governing body decide whether the facility will hold resident cash, and record the decision. If it will, the Administrator completes LIC 400 and obtains LIC 402 (SA-02) before holding any money. If it will not, residents or representatives are told at admission that the facility does not hold cash.
Residents keep and spend their own money. Staff never require a resident to hand over cash, a bank card or checks. Holding funds is done only on the resident's or representative's written request.

When funds are held, the business office issues a numbered, signed receipt for every deposit and withdrawal, gives the resident a copy, and keeps an individual ledger per resident showing date, amount, purpose and balance.

Held funds are kept in a separate account titled as the residents' money. They are never mixed with facility funds and never used for facility expenses. The Administrator reconciles the account and ledgers monthly and signs the reconciliation. The resident or representative may review the ledger on request.

At admission, a staff member and the resident (or representative) together prepare a written inventory of the resident's personal property, with item descriptions and condition. Both sign and date it. The original goes in the resident record (REC-01), and the resident or representative receives a copy.

Inventory modification: when property is added, removed, replaced or discarded, staff and the resident update the inventory the same day or the next business day, and both initial and date the change. The Administrator reviews every resident's inventory with the resident at least every 6 months and after any hospitalization or room move.

Marking of property: with the resident's consent, clothing is labeled with the resident's name using permanent markers, sewn-in or iron-on labels. Eyeglasses, hearing aids, dentures, walkers and electronics are marked or labeled and logged by description and serial number where available.

Secure area: each resident has a lockable drawer or cabinet in their room where practical. The facility also provides a locked central storage area at [LOCATION] for items the resident wants held. Keys or combinations are controlled by the Administrator and a designee, and each item placed in or taken from storage is logged and signed for.

Reporting a loss: when a resident, family member or staff member reports missing or damaged property, the staff member records it immediately and informs the Administrator the same day. The Administrator searches, interviews those involved, reviews the inventory and documents the findings within 3 business days.

The Administrator gives the resident or representative a written report of the result of the loss investigation. If theft is suspected, the Administrator informs the resident of the right to contact law enforcement and, if the facts suggest financial exploitation, reports under SP-01 immediately. The report is filed in the resident record and in the theft and loss log.

Death of a resident: on a resident's death, the Administrator or designee secures the room and the resident's property and locks the room. Two staff members, or one staff member and the representative, conduct a written inventory against the admission inventory and sign it. Any held funds are accounted for.

Property and funds of a deceased resident are released only to the authorized representative, executor or person entitled under the law, who signs a receipt. The release is documented and filed. The facility does not take, distribute or keep any property of a deceased resident.

Discharge or transfer: at discharge, the resident or representative and a staff member compare the property to the inventory, sign a release for all items and funds returned, and the Administrator files the signed release.

Staff may not borrow from, accept gifts above a nominal value from, or hold any property for residents except by the secure-storage procedure. Any violation is reported to the Administrator and handled under ST-06.
The Administrator trains all staff on this policy at orientation and annually (ST-03), and reviews the theft and loss log quarterly for patterns as part of quality assurance (GOV-03).

responsibilities.duty: Decide whether to hold cash, file LIC 400/402 if applicable, oversee inventories, investigate losses, reconcile resident accounts and manage release of property after death or discharge.
Issue receipts, keep ledgers and maintain the separate account for any held funds.
Assist with inventories, label property, report loss immediately and never take or borrow resident property.
Help prepare and review the inventory, tell staff of new items and report missing items promptly.

documentation: Signed inventory of personal property for each resident, with dated modifications

policies.title: Advance Directives and Resuscitation Requests
policies.applies_to: Administrator, all staff, residents and their representatives
policies.purpose: To respect each resident's decisions about future medical care, including requests regarding resuscitation, and to make sure staff know what to do in an emergency.
policies.policy: Residents have the right to refuse care (22 CCR §87468.1) and to make their own decisions about medical treatment. [AGENCY NAME] honors valid advance directives and resuscitative-measure requests as the California regulation on advance directives and resuscitative measures requires. Staff do not decide for a resident, and do not pressure a resident to sign or revoke a directive. Staff call 9-1-1 for any imminent threat to a resident's health (22 CCR §87465), except where the state regulation on resuscitative measures, as cross-referenced in the incidental medical care regulation, provides otherwise for a resident with a valid request. The directive or request is kept in the resident record and made available to staff and emergency responders. The Administrator checks the current text of the state advance-directive regulation when this policy is adopted and at each annual review under GOV-03.

definitions.definition: A written document in which a person names an agent to make health decisions and/or states wishes about future treatment.
A resident's request, such as a prehospital do-not-resuscitate form or a POLST, that CPR or other resuscitation not be attempted. It must be signed as the form and law require.
Physician Orders for Life-Sustaining Treatment, a signed medical order form that records a resident's treatment preferences.
A sudden condition that may cause serious harm or death if help is delayed, such as cardiac arrest, unresponsiveness, severe breathing difficulty or uncontrolled bleeding.

procedures: During pre-admission and at admission (AD-01), the Administrator or designee asks each resident whether they have an advance health care directive, a POLST, a prehospital DNR form or any other request about resuscitation. The question is asked of every resident and is not a condition of admission.

If the resident has any such document, staff obtain a copy and the Administrator checks that it appears complete and signed by the people the form requires. Staff do not give legal advice. A resident who wants to prepare a directive is referred to their physician, attorney or other appropriate resource.

The Administrator files the original or a copy in a consistent, easily found place in the resident record and notes in the record that one exists. Where the resident has a DNR or POLST form, a copy is also placed where emergency responders and staff can quickly find it, as the resident's representative and physician agree.
The Administrator names the agent or representative and their phone numbers on the face sheet in the resident record, so staff can contact them in an emergency.

All staff are told, at orientation and when a resident's status changes, where directives are kept and how to find them quickly. Direct care staff receive a shift report that identifies residents with resuscitative-measure requests.

In a medical emergency, the first staff member on scene checks the resident and calls 9-1-1 for any imminent threat to health, stays with the resident and gives first aid within their training. Staff then locate the directive or DNR form without delaying the call.

If a valid resuscitative-measure request is on file and the state regulation applies, staff follow the request and the regulation, call 9-1-1 as required, show the form to responders and notify the physician and representative. If the document is missing, unsigned or in doubt, staff begin resuscitation and call 9-1-1.
Staff hand the directive or request to emergency responders and send a copy with a resident who is transferred to a hospital, together with the face sheet and current medication list (HS-03).

A resident may change or revoke a directive at any time. When a resident tells staff of a change, staff tell the Administrator the same day, who gets the updated document, replaces the old one (keeping it marked superseded) and informs all shifts.

Staff do not witness, sign, interpret or complete a directive on a resident's behalf, and do not hold themselves out as able to do so. Staff never change a resident's wishes because of facility convenience or cost.

If a resident refuses care, staff respect the refusal, explain risks in plain terms, notify the physician and representative and document the refusal (HS-03). Refusal of care is not punished or used as a reason for discharge under AD-04.

At each Needs and Services Plan review (AD-02) and at least annually, the Administrator or designee asks the resident whether the directive is still current, and updates the record. The date of each check is recorded.
All staff are trained at orientation and annually on this policy and on locating and following directives (ST-03).
On the resident's death, the directive is handled under HS-06, and the original or copy remains in the resident record for the retention period (REC-01).

responsibilities.duty: Ask about directives at admission, file them, brief staff, verify the current regulation text each year, and ensure documents are updated and available.
Know where directives are kept, call 9-1-1 for an imminent threat to health, follow valid requests and give documents to responders.
Provide current documents and tell the facility of any change.
Sign and review medical orders such as POLST and advise on medical decisions.

documentation: Copy of each advance directive, POLST or prehospital DNR form in the resident record
Face sheet naming the agent or representative and their contact numbers
Record of the admission question and each annual or Needs and Services Plan check
Documentation of any refusal of care
Emergency event documentation showing 9-1-1 calls and documents provided to responders
Staff training records

policies.title: Privacy, Confidentiality and HIPAA
policies.applies_to: All staff, volunteers, contractors and residents of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To protect the privacy of residents' personal space and communications and the confidentiality of resident information, and to meet HIPAA requirements where they apply to the facility.
policies.policy: Residents have privacy in their use of the telephone, in their mail and in visits (22 CCR §87468.1). Privacy is also a requirement of the HCBS settings rule for residents who participate in the Medi-Cal Assisted Living Waiver (42 CFR 441.301(c)). Resident information is confidential. It is released only with the resident's or representative's consent or as the law permits, including to licensing, the Long-Term Care Ombudsman and emergency responders. [AGENCY NAME] will determine whether it is a HIPAA covered entity (45 CFR Parts 160 and 164), for example because it conducts standard electronic transactions such as Assisted Living Waiver billing. If it is, it designates a privacy officer, issues a Notice of Privacy Practices and follows the HIPAA Privacy and Security Rules. Paper and electronic records are secured, and any breach is reported to the Administrator immediately.

definitions.definition: Any information about a resident's identity, health, care, finances, family or behavior, in any form: spoken, written or electronic.

A health plan, health care clearinghouse or health care provider that transmits health information electronically in connection with a standard transaction (for example, billing a health plan or Medi-Cal). Such entities must comply with HIPAA.
Individually identifiable health information held or sent by a covered entity, in any form.
A written notice explaining how a covered entity uses and discloses PHI and what rights the individual has.
An unauthorized acquisition, access, use or disclosure of resident information.

procedures: Before licensure, the Administrator and governing body decide whether the facility is a HIPAA covered entity (for example, if it will bill Medi-Cal for the Assisted Living Waiver or conduct other standard electronic transactions) and record the decision and the reasons. The decision is reviewed annually and whenever billing practices change.

If the facility is a covered entity, the governing body designates a privacy officer ([PRIVACY OFFICER NAME], [PHONE]) in writing, adopts HIPAA privacy and security procedures, and issues a Notice of Privacy Practices. The Notice is given to each resident at admission and posted. Receipt is acknowledged in writing, and the refusal to sign is noted if it occurs.

Whether or not HIPAA applies, staff treat all resident information as confidential. They discuss a resident's information only with the resident, the authorized representative, and staff and providers who need it to give care, and never in public areas such as hallways or the dining room.

The Administrator keeps a list of persons each resident has authorized to receive information. Staff check the list before releasing information to family members, friends, visitors or telephone callers. If there is no authorization, staff do not confirm that the person is a resident, unless the law requires or allows.

Written consent is obtained before releasing information to people outside the care team. The consent states who may receive what information, for what purpose, and for how long, and is signed and dated. It is kept in the resident record and may be revoked at any time.

Information may be released without consent when the law permits or requires it, including to CDSS Community Care Licensing, the Long-Term Care Ombudsman, adult protective services or law enforcement for abuse reports, and emergency responders and treating providers in an emergency. The Administrator approves any other release and records what was released, to whom and why.

Residents may use the telephone and send and receive mail privately. Staff do not open, read or withhold a resident's mail, do not listen to calls and, where possible, provide a private place for calls and visits. Any assistance with mail or calls is given only on the resident's request.

Residents' personal space is respected. Staff knock and wait for a response before entering a resident's room, unless there is an emergency or a safety check required by the Needs and Services Plan. Personal care is given with doors or curtains closed and with the resident covered as much as possible.

If the facility serves residents under the Assisted Living Waiver, the Administrator ensures that privacy in the resident's living unit, including the lockable door where the resident wishes, is consistent with the HCBS settings rule, and that any limit on privacy is justified and documented in the person-centered plan as the waiver requires.

Paper records are kept in locked cabinets or a locked room, with access limited to staff who need them. Records are not left unattended in common areas. Resident names are not posted in public places except as needed for safety and with consideration of privacy (for example, a first name only on a meal list).

Electronic records and devices are protected with individual passwords, automatic screen locking and encryption where available. Staff do not share passwords, do not send resident information by personal email or text, and do not photograph residents or records with personal devices without consent.
Photographs, video, social media posts and marketing materials that show or identify a resident require the resident's or representative's prior written consent, and may be withdrawn at any time.
Staff sign a confidentiality statement at hire (ST-03, ST-05). The obligation continues after employment ends. Training on privacy and confidentiality is done at orientation and annually.

Any staff member who suspects or learns of a breach (for example, a lost chart, a misdirected fax, an unauthorized look at a record) reports it to the Administrator and privacy officer immediately. The Administrator investigates, limits further harm, tells the resident or representative, and, if the facility is a covered entity, handles notification as required by 45 CFR Part 164. The breach is documented.

Residents or representatives may ask to see or get a copy of the resident's record and may ask for corrections. The Administrator responds in writing within 30 days, or within the time HIPAA requires if it applies, and documents the request and response.
The privacy officer or Administrator reviews privacy practices, access lists and any breaches at least annually as part of GOV-03 quality assurance, and corrects any weaknesses.

responsibilities.duty: Decide covered-entity status, designate the privacy officer, adopt privacy and security procedures and approve corrective action after breaches.
Issue the Notice of Privacy Practices, manage authorizations and releases, secure records, train staff, investigate breaches and respond to record requests.
Keep resident information confidential, protect the privacy of the resident's phone calls, mail, visits and personal space, and report breaches immediately.
May decide who receives their information, review their records and raise privacy concerns under RR-02.

documentation: Documented determination of HIPAA covered-entity status
Privacy officer designation, if applicable
Notice of Privacy Practices and signed acknowledgments, if applicable
Resident authorization and consent forms, and revocations
Log of disclosures made outside of routine care
Staff confidentiality statements and training records
Breach reports and investigation records
Record access and amendment request log

policies.title: Nondiscrimination and Language Access
policies.applies_to: Administrator, all staff, volunteers and admissions personnel
policies.purpose: To make sure every applicant and resident of [AGENCY NAME] is treated with dignity and equality. This includes protection from discrimination in admission, transfer, discharge and room assignment, and access to services and information for residents with disabilities or limited English proficiency.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] does not discriminate in admission, transfer, discharge, room sharing, room or restroom assignment, use of a resident's preferred name or pronouns, or association with others, based on actual or perceived sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression or HIV status (22 CCR §87468.1(b)). The Department cannot waive this protection, and neither can [AGENCY NAME] or a resident through any agreement (22 CCR §87468.1(d)). The facility also does not discriminate on any other basis prohibited by state or federal law. This includes disability (ADA) and race, color or national origin (Title VI). The facility provides reasonable accommodation to residents with disabilities, including completion of LIC 9158 when the appraisal shows a hearing or other disability, as required by the admission agreement rules (22 CCR §87507). The facility provides qualified interpreters or translated documents to residents with limited English proficiency. Residents may not be asked to waive these protections in the admission agreement.

definitions.definition: A person's internal sense of gender and the way they outwardly present it. Both are protected, whether actual or perceived.

A change in rules, practices, communication or the physical environment that lets a resident with a disability use the home and its services equally, unless it would impose an undue burden or fundamentally alter the program.
A limited ability to speak, read, write or understand English well enough to take part in care decisions and understand facility documents.
The form required with the admission agreement when the appraisal shows a hearing or other disability.

procedures: The Administrator trains all staff on this policy at hire and at least annually. Training covers the protected categories, respectful use of names and pronouns, and the prohibition on retaliation. The training sign-in is kept in the personnel record.

Admissions staff apply the same written admission criteria (SB-06, AD-01) to every applicant. A decision not to admit must rest only on the applicant's care needs, the facility's license limits or the prohibited health conditions (AD-03). It may never rest on a protected characteristic.

HIV status, sexual orientation and gender identity or expression are never reasons to refuse admission, require a transfer or discharge, or restrict association with other residents. HIV status alone is not a prohibited health condition.

At admission, the resident is asked how they wish to be addressed, including preferred name and pronouns. The answer is recorded in the resident record and the needs and services plan (AD-02). All staff use it.

Room and restroom assignments and room-sharing decisions are made on the resident's stated needs and preferences and on safety. They are never made by sex assigned at birth, perceived orientation or HIV status. The Administrator reviews any proposed assignment that a staff member questions before it is carried out.
During the pre-admission appraisal, staff ask about hearing, vision, speech, mobility and communication needs and about the resident's preferred language. These are recorded on the appraisal.

When the appraisal shows a hearing or other disability, the Administrator completes LIC 9158 with the resident or representative and attaches it to the admission agreement. The accommodations are carried into the needs and services plan.

Staff may deliver reasonable accommodations such as large-print documents, written communication, assistive listening devices, accessible seating, help reading and signing documents, or a change in meal or activity setup. The Administrator approves any accommodation that needs a cost or a change to the building.

If a resident or representative asks for an accommodation, the Administrator responds within 2 business days, documents the request and the decision, and explains any denial in writing, with the reason and an alternative if one exists.

For a resident with LEP, staff identify the preferred language at the first contact and do not rely on guesses. The Administrator arranges a qualified interpreter, a bilingual staff member who is competent in the language, or a telephone interpreter service, [INTERPRETER SERVICE NAME / PHONE].

The admission agreement, grievance procedure, resident rights and notices of rate change or discharge are explained to the resident in the resident's language. They are given in translation where available, and in plain language, in 12-point type, as required for the agreement (22 CCR §87507).

Family members or other residents are not used as interpreters for consent, care, grievance or discharge discussions unless the resident asks for it. The request is documented, and a qualified interpreter is also offered.
Staff record each use of an interpreter or translated document, with the date, language and method, in the resident record.

The Administrator posts or gives each resident information about how to contact the CDSS Community Care Licensing Division and the Long-Term Care Ombudsman (1-800-231-4024) to report discrimination. Staff must not retaliate against anyone who complains (RR-02).

Any discrimination complaint is logged and reviewed by the Administrator within 3 business days under the grievance process in RR-02. The facility takes corrective action, including discipline of staff where warranted, and tells the resident the outcome.
The Administrator reviews admissions, discharges, room assignments and complaints each year to check for discriminatory patterns and updates training as needed (GOV-03).

responsibilities.duty: Enforces this policy, approves accommodations, arranges interpreters, completes LIC 9158, investigates complaints and keeps training records.
Apply admission criteria uniformly, ask about language, disability and preferred name and pronouns, and document the answers.
Use residents' preferred names and pronouns, deliver accommodations in the needs and services plan, and report suspected discrimination at once.
Supports resources for interpreters and accommodations and reviews annual findings.

documentation: Staff training sign-in on nondiscrimination and language access
Appraisal notes on disability and language
LIC 9158 where required
Preferred name and pronoun entries
Accommodation requests and responses
Interpreter and translation use log
Discrimination complaint log and outcomes

policies.title: Pre-Admission Screening, Appraisal and Reassessment
policies.applies_to: Administrator, admissions staff and staff who observe or care for residents
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] admits and keeps only residents whose needs it can safely meet. The facility does this by completing a pre-admission appraisal, obtaining a physician's medical assessment, screening for prohibited health conditions and reappraising residents over time.
policies.policy: No person is admitted until the facility has completed a pre-admission appraisal. The appraisal includes an interview and a functional, mental and social evaluation, obtains the applicant's consent, and ends in a written determination that the applicant is suitable under the admission criteria (22 CCR §87457). The facility obtains a physician's medical assessment and records the applicant's functional capabilities, mental condition and social factors, as required by the Title 22 appraisal provisions. Before accepting any resident, the facility screens for the prohibited health conditions (22 CCR §87615). Residents are reappraised on the schedule Title 22 requires and whenever staff observe a change in condition. Reappraisal also decides whether a resident with dementia needs awake night supervision. The facility will not admit a person whose needs it cannot meet, and it records the reason.

definitions.definition: The written evaluation completed before admission that covers the applicant's functional abilities, mental condition and social factors, with the applicant's consent, and leads to a suitability determination.
A review of the resident's needs done on the Title 22 schedule and whenever a change in condition is observed. It updates the appraisal and the needs and services plan.

A condition that bars admission or retention, including stage 3 and 4 pressure injuries, gastrostomy tubes, naso-gastric tubes, staph or other serious infection, total dependence on others for all ADLs, and tracheostomies. The list is not exhaustive (22 CCR §87615).
A staff person who is awake, rather than only on call, during the night. It is required if any resident with dementia needs it.

procedures: The Administrator, or a trained designee, takes each inquiry and gives the applicant and representative a plain-language description of the services provided, services not provided, and the conditions the facility cannot serve (SB-05, AD-03).
Before scheduling a visit or an admission, the Administrator records whether a bed is open and whether staffing and the building (including fire clearance status) match the applicant's likely needs.

The Administrator or designee interviews the applicant in person where possible, with the representative if the applicant agrees. The interview is held in the applicant's preferred language, with an interpreter if needed (RR-07).

The applicant, or the legal representative if the applicant cannot, signs a consent to the appraisal and to the collection of health information. Staff explain in plain language what will be shared and with whom (RR-06).

Staff complete the written functional evaluation (bathing, dressing, toileting, transferring, mobility, eating, continence), the mental evaluation (memory, orientation, behavior, wandering risk), and the social evaluation (history, supports, preferences, interests).

The Administrator obtains the physician's medical assessment from the applicant's physician and records the diagnoses, medications, allergies, dietary needs and any contagious or infectious disease, together with any limits on activity. The facility does not admit until the assessment is in hand.

The Administrator screens the appraisal and medical assessment against each prohibited health condition (22 CCR §87615) and against the restricted conditions that Title 22 permits only with an exception (AD-03). The screening is documented on the appraisal.

The Administrator checks the applicant's needs against the facility's staffing (ST-01), the building and the program description. This includes whether the applicant is nonambulatory or bedridden, which affects fire clearance, and whether dementia care or awake night supervision is required (HS-04).

The Administrator signs a dated, written suitability determination. The determination states either that the facility can meet the applicant's needs or the specific reasons it cannot. A person who cannot be admitted receives the reasons and, where possible, a referral to other resources.
Determinations rest only on care needs and license limits. They are never based on sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression or HIV status (RR-07).
If the appraisal shows a hearing or other disability, the Administrator completes LIC 9158 and attaches it to the admission agreement (22 CCR §87507).

The admission agreement is signed and dated within 7 days of admission, and the resident gets a copy immediately (RR-03, 22 CCR §87507). The appraisal, physician assessment and consent are placed in the resident record before or on the day of admission.
Within the first days of residency, the Administrator or designee builds the needs and services plan from the appraisal (AD-02).

Staff observe each resident daily and report any change in function, cognition, behavior, mood, weight, appetite, skin, continence or health to the Administrator the same shift. The Administrator decides whether a reappraisal is needed and starts it promptly.

Residents are reappraised on the schedule required by Title 22 and after any hospitalization, significant injury, fall with injury or other change in condition. The reappraisal is dated, signed and kept with the earlier appraisals.

At each reappraisal the Administrator re-screens for prohibited health conditions. If one is present, the Administrator follows AD-03 and AD-04, and informs the resident, representative and physician.

At each reappraisal, the Administrator also decides whether any resident with dementia needs awake night supervision. If so, the staffing schedule is changed before the next night shift and the change is documented (ST-01, HS-04).
The Administrator updates the needs and services plan after every reappraisal and reviews the plan with the resident and representative (AD-02).

responsibilities.duty: Completes or oversees all appraisals, signs the suitability determination, screens for prohibited conditions, decides on reappraisals and adjusts staffing.
Conduct inquiries and interviews, gather consents and records, and ensure documents are in the record before admission.
Observe residents daily and report changes of condition the same shift.
Provide accurate information, give consent, and take part in the interview and reappraisals.
Completes the medical assessment and updates it as the resident's condition changes.

documentation: Signed consent to appraisal
Pre-admission appraisal (interview, functional, mental and social evaluation)
Physician medical assessment
Prohibited-condition screening record
Dated suitability determination, or written reasons for non-admission
LIC 9158 where required
Reappraisal records
Awake-night supervision determination
Change-of-condition reports

policies.title: Needs and Services Plan
policies.applies_to: Administrator, direct care staff and the resident's representative
policies.purpose: To describe how [AGENCY NAME] writes, carries out and updates an individual needs and services plan for each resident, based on the appraisal, with the resident's participation.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] uses the California term 'needs and services plan'. Each resident has a written plan based on the pre-admission appraisal (22 CCR §87457) and each later reappraisal. The plan lists the basic services the facility provides (the services listed in LIC 604/604A) and any additional services the resident receives and pays for under the admission agreement (22 CCR §87507). The resident and the representative take part in decisions about the plan, and staff observe the resident and record changes, as Title 22 requires. The plan is updated at each reappraisal and whenever there is a change in condition.

definitions.definition: The written plan for one resident that lists identified needs, who will meet each need, how and how often, the resident's preferences and any accommodations.
The services every resident receives under the rates in the admission agreement, as listed in LIC 604/604A and the agreement.
Services beyond basic services that are listed in the admission agreement, with their rates.
A person the resident has authorized, or who is legally authorized, to act on the resident's behalf.

procedures: The Administrator starts the needs and services plan from the completed pre-admission appraisal and the physician's assessment, within the first days of residency and no later than the date of admission or the time the admission agreement is signed.

The Administrator invites the resident and, if the resident agrees or is unable to take part, the representative to a plan meeting. The meeting is held in the resident's preferred language, with an interpreter or accommodation where needed (RR-07).

The plan records each identified need: personal care, mobility and transfers, continence, nutrition and diet, medication assistance, cognitive and behavioral support, safety and wandering risk, social and activity needs, and communication or disability accommodations.

For each need the plan states who provides the service, how, how often and what the resident can do for themselves. It also states the resident's preferences, such as bathing time, meal choices, preferred name and pronouns, and daily routine.
The plan lists the basic services as described in LIC 604/604A and the admission agreement, and separately lists any additional services with their rates, so the plan and the agreement match (RR-03).
Where the plan includes medication assistance, the Administrator confirms that the physician's orders are on file and that trained staff are assigned (HS-01).
Where the appraisal shows a need the facility cannot meet, or a condition that is prohibited or restricted, the Administrator follows AD-03 and does not hide the need in the plan.

The resident or representative reviews the plan, may ask for changes, and signs and dates it. The refusal of a service or a disagreement with the plan is written in the plan and the Administrator explains the risk in plain language.
The resident is given a copy of the plan. The original is placed in the resident record (REC-01).
The plan is made available to every staff member who cares for the resident, either in a care summary or by directing staff to the record. Staff are shown any changes in the shift report.
Staff observe the resident during care and note any change in function, behavior, health or preferences in the daily record. They report it to the Administrator the same shift.
The Administrator reviews each reported change within 1 business day and decides whether to update the plan immediately, reappraise (AD-01) or contact the physician (HS-03).

At each reappraisal or change in condition, the Administrator updates the plan, dates the revision, reviews it with the resident and representative, and removes outdated entries so that only the current plan is in use.
The Administrator checks every plan for consistency with the admission agreement, staffing and the program description at least when each plan is updated, and corrects any gaps (GOV-03).

responsibilities.duty: Writes or oversees each plan, holds the plan meeting, reviews reported changes, updates the plan and checks it against the agreement.
Follow the plan, observe the resident, and document and report changes the same shift.
Take part in decisions, state preferences, and review and sign the plan and its updates.
Provide orders and information used in the plan and coordinate any outside services (HS-06).

documentation: Signed and dated needs and services plan and each revision
Record of the plan meeting and attendees
Interpreter or accommodation notes
Resident's refusals or disagreements
Daily observation notes and change-of-condition reports
Copy given to the resident or representative

policies.title: Retention Limits and Conditions the Facility Cannot Serve
policies.applies_to: Administrator, admissions staff, direct care staff and the licensee
policies.purpose: To state the health conditions [AGENCY NAME] cannot admit or retain, the fire clearance needed for nonambulatory or bedridden residents, and the hospice waiver. This keeps the facility within its license and keeps residents safe.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] does not admit or retain a resident who needs health services for, or who has, any of the following: stage 3 or 4 pressure injuries, gastrostomy tubes, naso-gastric tubes, staph or other serious infection, total dependence on others for all ADLs, or tracheostomies (22 CCR §87615). This list is not exhaustive. The facility treats any condition of similar acuity as requiring review against Title 22 before admission or continued stay. Title 22 also defines allowable and restricted health conditions and the exceptions that apply to them. The facility serves a resident with a restricted condition only when the Title 22 requirements for that exception are fully met and documented. A separate fire clearance is obtained before the facility accepts or keeps any nonambulatory or bedridden resident (22 CCR §87202). Hospice residents are served only under an approved hospice care waiver (22 CCR §87632).

definitions.definition: A condition that cannot be served in an RCFE. It includes stage 3 and 4 pressure injuries, gastrostomy tubes, naso-gastric tubes, staph or other serious infection, total dependence on others for all ADLs, and tracheostomies. The list is not exhaustive.
A resident who cannot walk or leave the building without help, or who is confined to bed. This requires a separate fire clearance before the resident is accepted or kept.
CDSS approval, requested in writing with a stated maximum number of hospice residents, that allows the facility to keep residents receiving hospice care.

procedures: The Administrator keeps a one-page list of the prohibited conditions at the admissions desk and reviews it with every admissions staff member at hire and annually.

At pre-admission screening (AD-01), the Administrator reviews the appraisal and physician assessment line by line for each prohibited condition and for any condition of similar acuity. A person with a prohibited condition is not admitted. The Administrator records the reason and gives the person and the referral source the reason in writing.

If an applicant's condition is restricted rather than prohibited, the Administrator confirms in writing that the Title 22 requirements for that condition are met before admission. If they are not met, the applicant is not admitted.

Staff observe residents daily for signs of a prohibited condition, such as a pressure injury that is worsening, a new feeding tube, a tracheostomy, a serious infection or loss of ability to do any ADL independently. They report suspected signs to the Administrator the same shift (HS-05, HS-03).
On any report, the Administrator contacts the resident's physician within 1 business day, or sooner if urgent, and requests an assessment and, where needed, a reappraisal (AD-01).

If a resident develops or is found to have a prohibited condition, the Administrator informs the resident, representative and physician. The Administrator also checks whether the condition can be corrected, such as by healing a wound, and plans an orderly transfer if it cannot, following AD-04 and the Title 22 relocation procedures.

The facility does not hide, delay documenting or work around a prohibited condition to keep a resident. The Administrator never allows staff to perform care that the facility's license does not allow.

Before accepting or keeping any nonambulatory or bedridden resident, the Administrator confirms that the facility's fire clearance covers such residents (22 CCR §87202). If it does not, the Administrator applies to the local fire authority and does not accept the resident until the clearance is in hand (SA-05, SP-06).

If a current resident becomes nonambulatory or bedridden and the fire clearance does not cover this, the Administrator takes immediate action to obtain it. The Administrator notifies the licensing analyst as required by REC-02 and arranges alternative placement if clearance cannot be obtained.

If the facility wishes to serve residents who are receiving hospice, the Administrator submits a written request for a hospice care waiver to CDSS that states the maximum number of hospice residents. CDSS decides within 30 days of an acceptable request (22 CCR §87632). The Administrator keeps the approved waiver on file.
The facility does not retain more hospice residents than the approved maximum and follows the conditions of the waiver. It coordinates care with the hospice agency (HS-06).
HIV status, sexual orientation and gender identity are not health conditions that bar admission or retention (RR-07).
Each year the Administrator reviews the list of prohibited and restricted conditions, the fire clearance and the hospice waiver for changes and documents the review (GOV-03).

responsibilities.duty: Screens every applicant and resident, decides on admission and retention, obtains the fire clearance and hospice waiver, and notifies the physician, representative and CDSS.
Apply the prohibited-condition list at every inquiry and refer questions to the Administrator.
Observe and report signs of prohibited conditions the same shift and never perform care outside the license.
Assesses the resident and advises on whether the condition is prohibited, restricted or resolved.
Ensures that the building, fire clearance and waivers match the residents served.

documentation: Prohibited-condition screening on each appraisal
Written reasons for non-admission
Physician assessments and condition reports
