Annual policy review record

policies.title: Discharge, Transfer and Relocation Notice
policies.applies_to: Administrator, admissions staff and direct care staff
policies.purpose: To set out how [AGENCY NAME] handles resident-initiated moves, evictions, Department-ordered relocations and health-condition relocations, so that residents get the notice and rights Title 22 requires and are never discharged for a prohibited reason.
policies.policy: A resident may move out at any time (22 CCR §87468.1). [AGENCY NAME] may require a resident to leave only on the grounds and by the procedures set out in the Title 22 eviction provisions, which may not be modified in the admission agreement. The admission agreement states the eviction grounds, the resident's notice rights and the right to contact CDSS and the Long-Term Care Ombudsman (22 CCR §87507). Department-ordered relocations and health-condition relocation orders, including a resident's right to request a review, follow the Title 22 provisions for those actions. No resident is transferred or discharged because of actual or perceived sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression or HIV status (22 CCR §87468.1(b)), and this protection cannot be waived (22 CCR §87468.1(d)).

definitions.definition: A facility-initiated discharge of a resident on grounds allowed by Title 22 and following the Title 22 notice procedure.
A move required by the Department, or because of a health condition the facility cannot serve, under the Title 22 relocation provisions.
The written notice to the resident and representative that states the reason, the effective date, the resident's rights and the contacts for CDSS and the Ombudsman.

procedures: Before taking any action to discharge or transfer a resident, the Administrator reviews the facts in writing. The Administrator confirms that the reason is a ground permitted under the Title 22 eviction provisions or a required relocation, and that no protected characteristic is involved (RR-07).

The Administrator tries to resolve the problem first where possible, such as by adjusting services, updating the needs and services plan (AD-02), involving the physician or family, or arranging added services. The efforts are documented.

For resident-initiated moves, staff accept the resident's notice, whether given in writing or not. The Administrator confirms the date with the resident, calculates any refund under the admission agreement (RR-03), and does not penalize the resident for leaving.

For a facility-initiated eviction, the Administrator prepares the written notice required by Title 22, stating the specific ground, the facts behind it and the effective date. The Administrator does not rely on any agreement provision that conflicts with the Title 22 eviction rules.

The notice is delivered to the resident and representative in person or as the rules require, in the resident's preferred language, and with an interpreter if needed (RR-07). It tells the resident of the right to contact CDSS Community Care Licensing and the Long-Term Care Ombudsman (1-800-231-4024).
The Administrator submits any report to CDSS that is required for the discharge or relocation and keeps a copy (REC-02).

For a Department-ordered relocation, the Administrator carries out the order within the timeframe given, informs the resident and representative the same day, and helps them find a suitable placement.

For a health-condition relocation, such as when a resident develops a prohibited condition (AD-03), the Administrator notifies the resident, representative and physician and explains the resident's right to request a review of the relocation order under Title 22. The Administrator helps the resident to file the request.

The Administrator helps the resident choose a new setting by providing a list of suitable options, sending records with the resident's consent (RR-06), arranging transport and passing on medication information. The Administrator also conducts a handoff to the receiving provider or family.

On the day of departure, staff return all of the resident's personal property and funds held, document them with the resident's signature (RR-04), and give the resident all medications ordered to go with them, with documentation of the release (HS-01).

For hospital transfers, staff follow HS-03. The facility does not use a hospital transfer to avoid Title 22 eviction procedures. The facility keeps the resident's room available as provided in the admission agreement and informs the resident of the terms.
The facility refunds money owed within the time stated in the admission agreement (RR-03).

The Administrator completes a discharge summary that states the reason, the date, the destination, the notices given, the property and money returned, and the follow-up. It is placed in the resident record and kept as in REC-01.
The Administrator reviews all discharges each quarter for patterns. Any sign of discrimination or of a discharge made outside the Title 22 grounds is corrected immediately (GOV-03).

responsibilities.duty: Decides on and carries out all discharges, relocations and notices, makes required reports to CDSS, and ensures rights and refunds are honored.
Report concerns that may lead to discharge early, help with packing and handoff, and never threaten or pressure a resident to leave.
Receive notice, give notice when moving, ask for review where available and receive belongings and funds.
Are available to residents to advise on and review discharge and relocation concerns.

documentation: Written review of the ground for discharge
Notice of discharge with proof of delivery
Interpreter or translation record
Department relocation orders and resident review requests
Reports to CDSS
Discharge summary
Property and funds return receipt
Medication release record
Refund calculation

policies.title: Medication Management, Assistance, Storage and Disposal
policies.applies_to: Administrator and all staff who assist residents with medications
policies.purpose: To make sure residents' medications are stored, assisted, recorded and destroyed safely and lawfully, and that only trained staff assist with them, within the limits of an RCFE license.
policies.policy: Staff of [AGENCY NAME] may assist only with medications that residents self-administer. Staff do not give injections unless authorized by law, and never force, hide or camouflage a medication (22 CCR §87465). A PRN medication may be assisted only under a signed and dated physician order on a prescription blank that states the symptoms, the exact dose, the minimum hours between doses and the maximum number of doses in 24 hours. Medications are stored centrally in a locked place in their original containers, and the medication record is kept at least 1 year. Destruction is done by the Administrator and one other non-resident adult, and the destruction record is kept at least 3 years. Staff who assist with medications complete the training required by HSC §1569.69: 10 hours of initial training and an exam for homes of 15 or fewer residents (6 hands-on hours before assisting and 4 within 2 weeks), and 8 hours each year. Homes of 16 or more residents require 24 hours initial training (16 hands-on, 8 within 4 weeks), an exam and 8 hours annually. Training is documented in the personnel record (22 CCR §87411).

definitions.definition: Helping a resident who is able to take their own medication, for example by reminding, opening containers, reading the label, handing the medication to the resident or steadying the resident's hand. The resident decides to take it.
A medication taken 'as needed' under a physician order that states the symptoms, the exact dose, the minimum hours between doses and the maximum doses per 24 hours.
Hiding medication in food or drink without the resident's knowledge. It is prohibited.
A locked place where medications are kept in their original containers, apart from the personal items of staff and other residents.

procedures: The Administrator keeps a written plan for incidental medical care and medication assistance (HS-02) and makes sure each resident's needs and services plan states whether the resident takes medication independently or needs assistance (AD-02).

Only staff who have completed the HSC §1569.69 training for this home's size may assist with medications. Before a new staff member's first assisted medication, the Administrator verifies that the required hands-on hours are complete: 6 hours for a home of 15 or fewer residents, or 16 hours for a home of 16 or more. The Administrator also schedules the remaining hours within the 2-week or 4-week deadline.
The Administrator confirms that each staff member passes the required exam, schedules the annual 8 hours of training, and files certificates and sign-in sheets in the personnel record (ST-05).

At admission, the Administrator obtains the physician's written orders and the original pharmacy-labeled containers for every medication. The Administrator compares the labels with the orders and records each medication, dose, route, time and prescriber. Any discrepancy is resolved with the physician or pharmacist before assistance begins.

Medications are stored in a locked central place, in their original containers. Medications needing refrigeration are kept in a locked container or locked refrigerator, separate from food. Only trained staff and the Administrator hold keys. Residents' medications are not mixed with those of other residents.

Staff wash hands and verify the resident's identity, the medication, the dose, the time and the route against the label and the record before each assistance. They then let the resident take the medication and watch it taken.

Staff never force a resident to take a medication and never hide or crush it into food or drink to conceal it. If a resident refuses, staff do not argue, record the refusal in the medication record, and tell the Administrator the same shift. The Administrator informs the physician when the refusal could affect the resident's health (HS-03).

Staff do not give injections unless the law authorizes it. Where an injection is needed, the Administrator arranges for a licensed professional, such as a home health nurse, to provide it under HS-02.

For each PRN medication, the Administrator confirms before assistance begins that there is a signed, dated physician order on a prescription blank that states the symptoms for use, the exact dose, the minimum hours between doses and the maximum doses per 24 hours. Orders lacking any element are not used. The Administrator asks the physician for a corrected order.
When a resident asks for a PRN medication, staff check the order, the time of the last dose and the daily maximum before assisting. Each use is recorded with the date, time, dose, symptom and result.
Staff record every assisted medication, refusal and omission immediately in the medication record, with the date, time, dose and staff initials. The medication record is kept at least 1 year.

If a medication error occurs, such as a wrong dose, missed dose or wrong resident, staff tell the Administrator at once. The Administrator contacts the physician or pharmacist, follows the instructions, observes the resident, completes an incident report (SP-02) and notifies the representative.

For an imminent threat to health, such as a severe reaction or overdose, staff call 9-1-1 first. Emergency numbers and the ambulance number are posted by the telephone, and a first aid kit is kept available (HS-03).

The Administrator and one other adult who is not a resident destroy discontinued, expired or deceased residents' medications. Destruction follows the pharmacy's and law's requirements for the type of medication. Both sign a destruction record that lists the resident, medication, strength, quantity, date and method. The record is kept at least 3 years.

When a resident leaves, only medications authorized by the physician and requested by the resident or representative go with the resident. The Administrator documents the release with a signature (AD-04).
The Administrator reviews medication records each month for gaps, errors and use of PRNs, checks locked storage and expired items, and takes corrective action (GOV-03).

responsibilities.duty: Ensures training and exams, obtains orders, controls storage and keys, reviews records monthly, oversees destruction and responds to errors.
Assist only with self-administered medications, follow the order and label, never force or hide, record each assistance, and report refusals and errors.
A non-resident adult who witnesses destruction and signs the record with the Administrator.
Provide written orders, including complete PRN orders, and answer questions on medications.
Decides whether to take medication, within the limits of the law and the physician's orders.

documentation: Physician orders, including PRN orders with all required elements
Medication record for each resident (kept at least 1 year)
Refusal and omission entries
Medication error and incident reports
Destruction record signed by two adults (kept at least 3 years)
Training certificates, hands-on hour logs and exam results for medication-assist staff
Monthly medication review notes

policies.title: Incidental Medical Care, Nursing Oversight and Delegation
policies.applies_to: All direct care staff, the Administrator, and any licensed nurse or contracted health professional serving residents of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To define the incidental medical and dental care [AGENCY NAME] provides, to keep staff within what an RCFE may lawfully do, and to set out how nursing oversight is obtained and how tasks are delegated or declined.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] maintains a written plan for incidental medical and dental care as required by 22 CCR §87465. Staff provide only incidental care that is allowed in a Residential Care Facility for the Elderly. Staff do not perform any service for a resident who has, or needs health services for, a prohibited health condition under 22 CCR §87615 (including stage 3 and 4 pressure injuries, gastrostomy tubes, naso-gastric tubes, staph or other serious infection, total dependence on others for all activities of daily living, and tracheostomies). That list is not exhaustive. Staff assist residents only with self-administered medications. Staff do not give injections unless authorized by law, and never force, hide or camouflage a medication. Care of healing wounds and of bedridden residents is provided only within the Department's regulations for those conditions, and the Administrator must verify the current requirements before the facility accepts or keeps a resident with either condition. If [AGENCY NAME] enrolls in the Medi-Cal Assisted Living Waiver, it will employ or have on call a licensed nurse. A first aid kit is kept on site, emergency numbers are posted, and an ambulance number is kept available. Staff call 9-1-1 for any imminent threat to a resident's health.

definitions.definition: Routine health-related assistance that an RCFE may lawfully provide, such as assistance with self-administered medications and first aid, as described in the facility's incidental medical and dental care plan.

A condition listed in 22 CCR §87615 for which a resident cannot be admitted or retained, including but not limited to stage 3 and 4 pressure injuries, gastrostomy tubes, naso-gastric tubes, staph or other serious infection, total dependence on others for all ADLs, and tracheostomies.
A medication the resident takes or applies personally, with staff providing only assistance permitted by 22 CCR §87465, such as reminding, opening containers or steadying the resident's hand.

Assigning a task to a staff member. At [AGENCY NAME], a task is assigned only if it falls within incidental care and the staff member has been trained for it. A task outside incidental care is never delegated to unlicensed staff.

procedures: The Administrator writes and keeps the Incidental Medical and Dental Care Plan, and reviews it at least annually and whenever services change. The plan is kept in the policy manual and available to staff and the licensing surveyor.

Before admission, the Administrator or designee screens the applicant against the prohibited health conditions in 22 CCR §87615 and records the result in the pre-admission appraisal (see AD-01). An applicant who needs a prohibited service is not admitted.

At every reappraisal and after any change of condition, the Administrator or designee rechecks the resident against the prohibited conditions and records the result in the needs and services plan (see AD-02 and HS-03).
If a resident develops a prohibited condition, the Administrator notifies the resident's physician and the person responsible and begins the discharge or transfer process in AD-03 and AD-04.
Staff assist only with self-administered medications, following HS-01. Staff do not give injections unless authorized by law, and never force, hide or camouflage a medication.

Before accepting a resident with a healing wound or who is bedridden, the Administrator confirms the applicable Department requirements and documents that the facility and the resident's physician or home health provider can meet them. Where a requirement cannot be met, the resident is not accepted or retained.

When a resident needs skilled care (for example, home health nursing or therapy), the care is provided by a licensed professional or agency under a physician's order, not by facility staff. The Administrator coordinates schedules and records the provider's name and contact information in the resident record.

Staff report any new wound, skin breakdown, swelling, pain, choking, or other change to the shift lead the same shift. The shift lead notifies the Administrator, and the Administrator decides whether the physician must be called (see HS-03).

Before assigning any task, the Administrator confirms it falls within incidental care and that the staff member has been trained and has demonstrated competence. Staff who are unsure decline the task and ask the Administrator.

If [AGENCY NAME] enrolls in the Assisted Living Waiver, the Administrator designates a licensed nurse (employed or on call) with name and [PHONE] posted at the staff station, and records nursing oversight visits and consultations in the resident record.
The Administrator keeps a stocked first aid kit in a known, accessible location on each floor, and checks it monthly. The check date and any replaced items are logged.
Emergency numbers (9-1-1, poison control, ambulance, physician contacts, licensing office, Administrator [PHONE]) are posted by each telephone, and an ambulance number is kept available.

For any imminent threat to health (such as unresponsiveness, chest pain, stroke symptoms, severe bleeding or breathing difficulty), staff call 9-1-1 first, start first aid within their training, and then notify the Administrator and the person responsible.
Staff who give first aid hold current first aid certification. The Administrator checks certification dates quarterly (see ST-03).

Staff who perform a task outside their allowed scope, or who see another staff member do so, report it to the Administrator immediately. The Administrator investigates, retrains or disciplines as needed, and documents the outcome.
The Administrator reviews incidental care practices at the quarterly quality review (see GOV-03) and corrects any gap found.

responsibilities.duty: Maintains the incidental care plan, screens for prohibited conditions, decides what the facility may accept, ensures nursing oversight if waiver-enrolled, and keeps the first aid kit and emergency numbers current.
Provides nursing consultation, oversight and training within the nurse's scope of practice as arranged by the Administrator.
Provide only allowed assistance, report changes of condition the same shift, call 9-1-1 for imminent threats, and decline tasks outside their scope.

responsibilities.role: Resident's physician and home health or hospice provider
responsibilities.duty: Order and provide skilled care and communicate changes to the Administrator.

documentation: Incidental Medical and Dental Care Plan with review dates
Pre-admission appraisal and reappraisal showing prohibited-condition screening
Needs and services plan entries for health services
First aid kit check log
Posted emergency number list
Staff first aid certification records
Nursing oversight records, if waiver-enrolled
Records of tasks declined or corrected

policies.title: Change of Condition, Physician Notification and Hospital Transfer
policies.applies_to: All staff, the Administrator and the contracted physicians and health providers of [AGENCY NAME] residents
policies.purpose: To ensure that any change in a resident's condition is recognized quickly, that emergency help is summoned when needed, that the physician and the person responsible are told, that the resident is reappraised, and that required reports reach the state on time.
policies.policy: Staff call 9-1-1 for any imminent threat to a resident's health (22 CCR §87465). For any other change of condition, staff notify the Administrator, and [AGENCY NAME] notifies the resident's physician and the person responsible for the resident. After any change of condition, the resident is reappraised and rechecked against the prohibited health conditions in 22 CCR §87615. [AGENCY NAME] sends a written report to the licensing agency and the person responsible within 7 days of any death, any serious injury as determined by the physician, any use of an AED, and any incident threatening the welfare, safety or health of a resident, including unexplained absence or psychological abuse (22 CCR §87211(a)(1)). Outbreaks, poisonings, catastrophes and major accidents are reported by phone or fax to the licensing agency and the local health officer within 24 hours (22 CCR §87211(a)(2)). Fires and explosions are reported immediately to the local fire authority and no later than the next working day to the licensing agency (22 CCR §87211(a)(3)).

definitions.definition: Any noticeable change in a resident's physical, mental, emotional or functional status, such as a fall, new confusion, loss of appetite, new pain, skin change, fever, or a decline in ability to perform activities of daily living.
The resident's representative, family member, conservator or other person named in the admission agreement to be contacted about the resident's care.
An injury that the resident's physician determines to be serious.
A situation in which delay in care could cause death or serious harm, such as unresponsiveness, chest pain, stroke symptoms, severe bleeding or difficulty breathing.

procedures: Any staff member who sees a possible imminent threat to health calls 9-1-1 immediately, stays with the resident, gives first aid within their training, and then notifies the Administrator.
For other changes of condition, the staff member tells the shift lead right away and writes the observation (what, when, who noticed) in the resident's record before the end of the shift.

The shift lead or Administrator contacts the resident's physician the same day, or immediately if symptoms are severe or worsening, and records the date, time, who was spoken to and instructions given. Any physician order is written down and read back.
The shift lead or Administrator notifies the person responsible the same day, and records the date, time and person reached. If no one can be reached, attempts are logged and repeated.

When a resident is sent to the hospital, staff send the face sheet, current medication list, physician and responsible-person contacts, advance directive or POLST (see RR-05), and a short written description of the change. If possible, a staff member accompanies the resident or follows up by phone.
Staff record the hospital name, time of departure, and who was notified. The Administrator or designee calls the hospital the next day to check status and expected discharge.

On return from the hospital or any acute illness, the Administrator or designee reviews discharge instructions and medication changes with the physician or discharge nurse, updates the medication records (see HS-01), and arranges any ordered home health.

Within 7 days of any change of condition, and before the resident returns from a hospital stay when possible, the Administrator completes a reappraisal and updates the needs and services plan (see AD-01 and AD-02).

At each reappraisal, the Administrator rechecks the resident against the prohibited conditions in 22 CCR §87615. If one is present or newly needed, the Administrator consults the physician and the person responsible and starts the process in AD-03 and AD-04 without delay.

The Administrator decides whether the event requires a state report. Death, serious injury as determined by the physician, AED use, or any incident threatening welfare, safety or health, including unexplained absence or psychological abuse, requires a written report to the licensing agency and the person responsible within 7 days.

For an outbreak, poisoning, catastrophe or major accident, the Administrator reports by phone or fax to the licensing agency and the local health officer within 24 hours. Contact numbers are kept at the Administrator's desk: licensing office [LICENSING REGIONAL OFFICE PHONE], local health officer [LOCAL HEALTH OFFICER PHONE].
For a fire or explosion, staff call the local fire authority immediately. The Administrator notifies the licensing agency no later than the next working day.

If the change of condition involves suspected abuse, the Administrator follows SP-01, and if the incident is also reportable, follows SP-02 and REC-02. The staff member does not wait for the 7-day report to make time-sensitive reports.
The Administrator keeps a copy of every report sent, with proof of date and method (fax confirmation, email, or delivery receipt), in the incident file.
Staff increase observation of the resident after a change of condition as ordered by the physician or directed by the Administrator, and record each check.
The Administrator reviews all changes of condition, transfers and reports monthly for trends and uses the results at the quarterly quality review (see GOV-03).

responsibilities.duty: Recognize and report changes, call 9-1-1 for imminent threats, and document observations.
Contact the physician and person responsible, coordinate hospital transfer, and brief the Administrator.
Ensures reappraisal and prohibited-condition recheck, decides on and submits required reports to licensing and the local health officer, and keeps proof of reporting.
Evaluates the resident, gives orders and determines whether an injury is serious.

documentation: Change of condition entry in the resident record
Physician and responsible-person notification log
Hospital transfer packet checklist and hospital follow-up notes
Reappraisal and updated needs and services plan
Prohibited-condition recheck
Written 7-day reports and 24-hour phone or fax report records with confirmation
Fire or explosion reports to the fire authority and licensing agency
Monthly trend review

policies.title: Dementia and Memory Care
policies.applies_to: The Administrator, all direct care staff and any staff who work with residents who have dementia at [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To make sure residents with dementia are admitted only when [AGENCY NAME] can safely meet their needs, are supervised appropriately day and night, and are cared for by trained staff under a written dementia program if dementia care is advertised.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] admits and keeps a resident with dementia only when the pre-admission appraisal and reappraisals show that the facility can meet the resident's needs. In a home with fewer than 16 beds, at least one night staff person is awake and on duty whenever a resident with dementia needs awake night supervision, as shown by appraisal, reappraisal or observation (22 CCR §87705). Night supervision otherwise meets 22 CCR §87415: for fewer than 16 residents, a qualified person is on call on the premises overnight; for 16 to 100 residents, one employee is awake on duty and one is on call within 10 minutes. Night staff know the emergency plan and are first aid trained. If [AGENCY NAME] advertises dementia special care, it maintains a written dementia program covering philosophy, admission, training, activities, environment, changes in condition and success indicators, and keeps its advertisements for 3 years (22 CCR §87706). Direct care staff complete 12 hours of dementia training initially and 8 hours annually (HSC §1569.626), and the Administrator's continuing education includes 8 hours on dementia.

definitions.definition: A condition marked by decline in memory, thinking or judgment that interferes with daily living, as diagnosed by a physician or shown by appraisal.
A staff person who is awake, alert and on duty throughout the night and is able to observe and respond to residents.
The written program [AGENCY NAME] must keep if it advertises dementia care.
Measures the facility uses to judge whether its dementia program is working, such as fewer falls, fewer unmet needs or resident and family satisfaction.

procedures: The Administrator decides before opening whether [AGENCY NAME] will advertise dementia or memory care. If it will, the Administrator writes the dementia program before any advertisement is published.

The written dementia program describes the facility's philosophy of care, admission criteria and process, staff training, activities, the physical environment, how changes in condition are handled, and the indicators of success. The Administrator reviews and updates it annually (see GOV-03).
The Administrator keeps a copy of every advertisement, brochure, web page and listing that refers to dementia care, with the date it ran, in a file kept for 3 years.

At pre-admission, the Administrator or designee assesses cognition, wandering risk, behaviors, night waking and need for supervision, and records the findings in the appraisal (see AD-01). A resident whose needs exceed what the facility can safely meet is not admitted (see AD-03).

The needs and services plan for each resident with dementia states the resident's routines, communication approaches, triggers, safety needs, wandering risk and level of night supervision (see AD-02).

The Administrator decides at appraisal, at each reappraisal, and whenever staff report night observations whether a resident with dementia needs awake night supervision. The decision and reasons are written in the resident record.

While any resident needs awake night supervision, at least one night staff person is awake and on duty all night. The Administrator schedules to this requirement and does not allow the night person to be reassigned or to sleep (see ST-01).
Night staff know the facility emergency plan and hold current first aid training. The Administrator checks this before assigning the person to nights.

Each direct care staff member completes 12 hours of dementia training initially and 8 hours each year. The Administrator tracks dates and hours on the training log and schedules makeup training for anyone behind (see ST-03).
The Administrator completes dementia-related continuing education, including 8 hours on dementia, as part of administrator certification renewal (see SB-02).
Staff use calm, non-confrontational approaches and redirection. Restraints or locked confinement are not used to manage behavior (see SP-04 and SP-03).
Staff offer meaningful activities matched to each resident's abilities and history each day, and record participation (see DL-02).

The Administrator keeps the environment safe, with clear walkways, adequate lighting, secure hazardous items and alarms or other monitoring that does not violate residents' rights, and checks these weekly.

When a resident with dementia changes (new wandering, aggression, decline in function), staff report it the same shift. The Administrator reappraises, informs the physician and person responsible, and updates the plan (see HS-03).
If a resident's needs go beyond what the facility can safely meet, the Administrator starts the process in AD-03 and AD-04.
At the quarterly quality review, the Administrator reviews the dementia program's success indicators and corrects gaps.

responsibilities.duty: Writes and updates the dementia program, decides on awake night supervision, schedules night staff, tracks training and keeps advertisements for 3 years.
Complete required dementia training, follow each resident's plan, and report changes.
Stay awake and on duty when required, know the emergency plan and be trained in first aid.
Provide diagnosis, orders and information that help the facility plan care.

documentation: Written dementia program (if dementia care is advertised) and annual review
Advertisement file kept for 3 years
Appraisals, reappraisals and night supervision determinations
Needs and services plans for residents with dementia
Night staffing schedules
Staff dementia training log (12 hours initial, 8 hours annual) and certificates
Administrator CE records
Quarterly review of success indicators

policies.title: Falls Prevention and Skin Integrity
policies.applies_to: All direct care staff, maintenance staff and the Administrator of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To reduce falls and skin breakdown by assessing risk early, planning individualized prevention, keeping the building safe, and making sure residents with conditions the facility cannot serve are not admitted or retained.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] assesses each resident's risk of falls and skin breakdown at appraisal and at every reappraisal and records the risk and prevention measures in the needs and services plan. A resident with a stage 3 or 4 pressure injury cannot be admitted or retained (22 CCR §87615). The building is maintained to the standards of 22 CCR §87303, including grab bars at toilets, tubs and showers, non-slip surfaces and emergency lighting, and hot water kept between 105°F and 120°F. Postural supports are used only as the Department's postural support requirements allow (see SP-04). Staff receive 4 hours of training on postural supports, restricted health conditions and hospice.

definitions.definition: An unintended event in which a resident comes to rest on the floor or another lower surface, whether or not injured and whether or not witnessed.
Damage to skin and underlying tissue from pressure or friction, staged 1 to 4 by depth. Stage 3 and 4 injuries are prohibited conditions under 22 CCR §87615.
The condition of a resident's skin, including color, warmth, moisture, redness, breaks, bruises and wounds.
A device used to maintain a resident's position or balance, governed by the Department's postural support requirements and SP-04.

procedures: At pre-admission appraisal, the Administrator or designee screens each applicant for fall history, gait and balance, vision, footwear, medications that affect balance, continence, cognition, and current skin condition, and records the findings (see AD-01).
If an applicant has a stage 3 or 4 pressure injury, the Administrator does not admit the applicant and refers the applicant to a suitable provider (see AD-03).

The needs and services plan records each resident's fall and skin risk and the specific prevention measures, such as assistance with walking, a call method, toileting schedule, repositioning prompts, hygiene routine and skin checks (see AD-02).
At each reappraisal and after any fall, hospitalization or change of condition, the Administrator or designee repeats the risk assessment and updates the plan (see HS-03).

Staff help residents with bathing and dressing and observe the skin. Any redness that does not fade, open area, blister, bruise, swelling or new pain is reported to the shift lead the same shift and written in the record.
The shift lead tells the Administrator, who contacts the physician and person responsible (see HS-03). Staff do not treat wounds beyond what the Department allows (see HS-02).
If a resident develops a stage 3 or 4 pressure injury, the Administrator consults the physician and person responsible and starts the process in AD-03 and AD-04.

After any fall, staff check the resident without moving anyone who may be seriously hurt, call 9-1-1 if there is an imminent threat to health, notify the Administrator, and record the time, place, circumstances, injuries and witnesses on the incident report (see SP-02).

The Administrator reports a fall to the physician and person responsible, and sends the written report required by 22 CCR §87211 within 7 days if the physician determines the injury is serious (see REC-02).
After every fall, the Administrator or designee reviews causes (footwear, lighting, medications, furniture, supervision) and changes the plan or environment, and records what was done.

Maintenance staff or the Administrator inspect grab bars at toilets, tubs and showers, non-slip surfaces and flooring, and emergency lighting at least monthly. Hot water is tested monthly at resident-use fixtures to keep it between 105°F and 120°F. Results and repairs are logged (see DL-03).
Staff keep hallways, exits and bathrooms free of clutter and spills, and clean spills right away. Residents' walkers, canes, glasses and call devices are kept within reach.
Postural supports are used only on a physician's written order, in line with the Department's requirements, and are never used for staff convenience or discipline (see SP-04).
The Administrator makes sure staff complete the required 4 hours of training on postural supports, restricted health conditions and hospice, and records completion (see ST-03).
The Administrator reviews falls and skin problems each quarter for patterns and reports results at the quality review (see GOV-03).

responsibilities.duty: Completes appraisals and reappraisals, rejects or begins discharge for prohibited conditions, ensures plant safety and staff training, and reviews falls and skin problems.
Follow plans, observe skin and mobility, report changes the same shift and document falls.
Inspect and repair grab bars, flooring, lighting and hot water temperature and log the work.
Evaluates injuries and wounds and writes orders.

Needs and services plans with prevention measures
Skin change and fall entries in resident records
Incident reports and post-fall reviews
Monthly safety inspection log (grab bars, surfaces, emergency lighting, hot water temperature)
Postural support orders, if any
Staff training records for the 4-hour postural supports/restricted conditions/hospice course
Quarterly review notes

policies.title: Hospice, Home Health Coordination and Death of a Resident
policies.applies_to: The Administrator, direct care staff and the hospice and home health providers serving residents of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To set out how [AGENCY NAME] obtains authority to serve residents on hospice, coordinates hospice and home health care with the facility's own plan, protects hospice residents during an evacuation, and handles a resident's death with dignity, reporting and safeguarding of property.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] allows residents to receive hospice and home health services in the facility only within the Department's requirements. Before the facility serves residents on hospice, it holds the required hospice care waiver. The Administrator submits a written request that states the maximum number of hospice residents, and CDSS decides within 30 days of an acceptable request (22 CCR §87632). Hospice care also follows the Department's other hospice requirements. Hospice and home health plans of care are coordinated with the resident's needs and services plan. If the facility evacuates or relocates residents, it notifies each hospice resident's hospice agency (22 CCR §87212). A death is reported in writing to the licensing agency and the person responsible within 7 days (22 CCR §87211(a)(1)). The resident's personal property is safeguarded and inventoried (see RR-04). Staff call 9-1-1 for any imminent threat to health (22 CCR §87465).

definitions.definition: A licensed program that provides comfort-focused, end-of-life care for a resident with a terminal illness under a physician's certification.
CDSS approval, requested in writing under 22 CCR §87632, that allows the facility to serve hospice residents up to a stated maximum number.
A licensed provider that delivers skilled nursing, therapy or other health services to a resident in the facility under a physician's order.
The resident's representative, family member, conservator or other person named in the admission agreement.

procedures: If [AGENCY NAME] intends to serve residents on hospice, the Administrator submits a written request for a hospice care waiver to CDSS stating the maximum number of hospice residents the facility will serve, and keeps a copy and proof of submission.

The Administrator tracks the CDSS response, which is due within 30 days of an acceptable request. The facility does not accept a resident for hospice care until the waiver is granted, and never serves more hospice residents than the approved maximum.

When a resident or the person responsible chooses hospice, the Administrator obtains the name and contact information of the hospice agency, a copy of the hospice plan of care, and the physician's orders, and files them in the resident record.

The Administrator, the hospice team and the resident or person responsible meet to coordinate roles. They decide who provides each service, how staff will communicate with the hospice nurse, and how symptoms and changes will be reported. The agreed plan is added to the needs and services plan (see AD-02).

Direct care staff are told what they may and may not do for hospice residents. Staff provide only incidental care and assistance within their scope and never perform skilled tasks that belong to hospice or home health staff (see HS-02).

The Administrator reappraises the resident when hospice starts and whenever condition changes, and rechecks against prohibited health conditions (see AD-01 and HS-03). If the resident's needs cannot be met under the Department's requirements, the Administrator works with the hospice, physician and person responsible on transfer (see AD-03 and AD-04).

For residents receiving home health, the Administrator records the provider, visit schedule, orders and contact person, and requires visit notes or summaries to be shared with the facility so medications and care orders stay consistent (see HS-01).

The emergency disaster plan identifies each hospice resident. If residents are evacuated or relocated, the Administrator or designee notifies each hospice resident's hospice agency, and the notice is documented with time and person contacted (see SP-05).

At the time of a death, staff call 9-1-1 if the death is unexpected or if instructed to by the physician or hospice, and call the hospice nurse if the resident is on hospice. Staff do not move or release the body except as directed by the physician, hospice, or authorities.
Staff notify the Administrator immediately. The Administrator notifies the physician and the person responsible as soon as possible and records the time, who was told, and the instructions received.
The Administrator sends a written report of the death to the licensing agency and the person responsible within 7 days, and keeps a copy with proof of delivery (see REC-02).

The Administrator secures the resident's room and valuables, and with a second staff member inventories personal property and any funds held, signs and dates the inventory, and follows RR-04 for release to the person responsible or legal representative.
Medications of a deceased resident are removed from use and handled under the facility's medication storage and destruction procedure (see HS-01).
Staff treat the resident, family and other residents with respect after a death, offer support and, where appropriate, give residents an opportunity to say goodbye or to take part in a remembrance.
The Administrator completes any required resident record entries, processes the final billing and refund under the admission agreement (see RR-03), and files the record under REC-01.
The Administrator reviews each death and each hospice episode afterward to see whether care could be improved, and records any follow-up.

responsibilities.duty: Requests and tracks the hospice waiver, coordinates with hospice and home health, notifies hospice during evacuation, makes the 7-day death report and ensures property is inventoried and safeguarded.
Provide permitted assistance, communicate with hospice and home health staff, call 9-1-1 or hospice at the time of death as directed and protect the resident's property.
Deliver skilled and comfort care, share care plans and visit notes and respond to symptom calls.
Writes orders, certifies hospice eligibility and pronounces or confirms death as required.

documentation: Written hospice waiver request, proof of submission and CDSS response
Hospice and home health plans of care, orders and contact lists
Coordinated needs and services plan
Hospice notification record for any evacuation or relocation
Death record, notifications log and 7-day written report to licensing and the person responsible
Signed personal property inventory and release record
Medication disposition record
Post-death review notes

policies.title: Abuse, Neglect and Exploitation Prevention and Reporting
policies.applies_to: All employees, volunteers and contractors of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To protect residents from abuse, neglect and exploitation, to ensure every staff member knows how and when to report suspected abuse, and to guarantee that reports are made on time, evidence is preserved and no one is punished for reporting.
policies.policy: Residents of [AGENCY NAME] have the right to be treated with dignity and to be free from punishment, humiliation, intimidation and abuse (22 CCR §87468.1). All staff are mandated reporters of elder and dependent adult abuse under W&I Code §15630. Staff report by phone immediately or as soon as practicably possible, and follow with a written report on form SOC 341 within the statutory time. For suspected physical abuse, the report goes to the local ombudsman, the licensing agency and local law enforcement within 2 hours if there is serious bodily injury, and otherwise within 24 hours (22 CCR §87211(b),(c)). An incident threatening the welfare, safety or health of a resident, including psychological abuse, is also reported in writing to the licensing agency and the person responsible within 7 days (22 CCR §87211(a)(1)). The Long-Term Care Ombudsman CRISISline is 1-800-231-4024. [AGENCY NAME] protects residents from further harm, preserves evidence and does not retaliate against anyone who reports in good faith. Staff do not need the Administrator's permission to report and may not be told to delay or withhold a report.

definitions.definition: A person who is required by W&I Code §15630 to report suspected elder or dependent adult abuse. This includes care custodians and facility staff.
Physical abuse, sexual abuse, psychological or emotional abuse, neglect, abandonment, isolation, financial exploitation and other treatment that causes harm or suffering to a resident.

An injury involving extreme physical pain, substantial risk of death, protracted loss or impairment of a bodily function, or injury requiring medical intervention such as surgery, hospitalization or physical rehabilitation.
The written report form used to report suspected abuse of an elder or dependent adult.
Any adverse action, such as firing, discipline, schedule changes, threats or harassment, taken because someone made or supported a report.

procedures: The Administrator trains every new employee on this policy during orientation and before the employee works alone, and refreshes the training at least annually. Each employee signs an acknowledgment that they are a mandated reporter and understand how to report (see ST-03).

The facility posts the Long-Term Care Ombudsman CRISISline (1-800-231-4024), the local ombudsman number [LOCAL OMBUDSMAN PHONE], the licensing office number [LICENSING REGIONAL OFFICE PHONE] and local law enforcement number where residents, families and staff can see them. Residents are told at admission how to complain to the licensing agency and the ombudsman (see RR-02).

Any staff member who sees, hears of or suspects abuse, neglect or exploitation protects the resident first. The staff member separates the resident from the alleged abuser, calls 9-1-1 if anyone is in danger or injured, and gets medical care if needed.

The staff member makes the report personally. For suspected physical abuse with serious bodily injury, the staff member or Administrator reports by phone to the local ombudsman, the licensing agency and local law enforcement within 2 hours. For suspected physical abuse without serious bodily injury, the reports are made within 24 hours.

For other suspected abuse, such as neglect, sexual, psychological or financial abuse, the staff member reports by phone immediately or as soon as practicably possible to the agencies required by W&I Code §15630. If unsure which category applies, the staff member reports right away and asks the agency.

The staff member completes and sends the written SOC 341 within the time the statute requires. The Administrator helps but does not edit or hold back the report. Each mandated reporter remains responsible for making sure their own report is made.

The Administrator is told as soon as possible. The Administrator notifies the person responsible for the resident and the resident's physician, unless the person responsible is the suspected abuser, in which case the Administrator asks the investigating agency how to proceed.

The Administrator sends the written report to the licensing agency and the person responsible within 7 days for any incident threatening the resident's welfare, safety or health, including psychological abuse (see SP-02 and REC-02).

Staff and the Administrator preserve evidence. They do not clean or alter the scene, they keep clothing, bedding and items as they are, they photograph visible injuries when permitted, and they list witnesses and write down what was seen and heard in the staff member's own words, with date and time.

An employee accused of abuse is immediately removed from resident contact and from the shift pending investigation. The Administrator does not question the resident in a way that could influence the investigation, and cooperates with law enforcement, licensing and the ombudsman.

The Administrator offers the resident medical evaluation, emotional support, a safe room or caregiver assignment, and checks on the resident daily until the matter is resolved. The resident is allowed private contact with the ombudsman and advocates.

The facility does not retaliate against any resident, family member or staff member who reports or cooperates. Retaliation is grounds for discipline up to termination. Any suspected retaliation is reported to the Administrator or directly to the licensing agency.
If the Administrator is the suspected person, staff report directly to the agencies and the governing body (see GOV-01).

After an investigation, the Administrator takes corrective action, which can include retraining, discipline, termination, changes to supervision or the environment, and updates to care plans, and documents the outcome. Findings against an employee are handled under the personnel policies (see SB-03 and ST-06).
The Administrator keeps all reports, SOC 341 forms, correspondence and records of actions in a confidential incident file, with copies of proof of submission.
The Administrator reviews all abuse and neglect reports and near misses quarterly to find patterns and improve prevention (see GOV-03).

responsibilities.duty: Protect residents, report suspected abuse within the required times, complete SOC 341 and cooperate with investigators, without needing permission.
Train staff, post numbers, ensure reports are made, notify the person responsible, send the 7-day written report, remove accused staff from contact, preserve evidence and prevent retaliation.
Receives reports involving the Administrator and ensures corrective action.

responsibilities.role: Ombudsman, licensing agency and law enforcement
responsibilities.duty: Receive reports, investigate and advise on protective steps.

documentation: Mandated reporter acknowledgments and training records
Posted ombudsman, licensing and law enforcement numbers
Phone report log showing agency, person, date and time
SOC 341 forms and proof of submission
7-day written reports to licensing and the person responsible
Evidence preservation notes and witness statements
Resident protection and follow-up record
Investigation findings and corrective actions
Quarterly review of reports

policies.title: Incident and Accident Reporting
policies.applies_to: All staff, volunteers, the Administrator and the governing body of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To make sure every death, injury, accident, outbreak, fire and other reportable event at [AGENCY NAME] is responded to, documented and reported to the correct agency and to the person responsible for the resident within the time California requires.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] reports events exactly as required by 22 CCR §87211. (1) Written report within 7 days: we send a written report to the licensing agency and to the person responsible for the resident within 7 days of any death, any serious injury as determined by the physician, any use of an automated external defibrillator (AED), and any incident that threatens the welfare, safety or health of a resident, including an unexplained absence or psychological abuse. (2) Within 24 hours: outbreaks, poisonings, catastrophes and major accidents are reported by phone or fax to the licensing agency and the local health officer. (3) Fires and explosions are reported immediately to the local fire authority and no later than the next working day to the licensing agency. (4) Suspected physical abuse of an elder or dependent adult is reported to the local ombudsman, the licensing agency and local law enforcement within 2 hours if there is serious bodily injury and otherwise within 24 hours. (5) Financial and administrative events: we give written notice to the licensing agency within 2 business days of receiving a foreclosure notice, unlawful detainer, bankruptcy filing, rent default notice or utility shut-off notice, and we tell applicants before they sign an admission agreement. Failure to give this notice carries a civil penalty of $100 per day, up to $2,000. We also notify the licensing agency of a new administrator within 30 days and of a change of chief corporate officer within 15 working days. No staff member may delay, soften or withhold a report. When there is doubt, we report.

definitions.definition: Any event listed in 22 CCR §87211, including a death, a serious injury as determined by the physician, AED use, an unexplained absence, psychological abuse or any other event that threatens the welfare, safety or health of a resident.
The resident's authorized representative, conservator, agent under a power of attorney, family member or placement agency identified in the admission agreement and the resident record.
California Department of Social Services, Community Care Licensing Division, Adult and Senior Care Program, through the regional office that serves [ADDRESS].

An injury involving extreme physical pain, substantial risk of death, protracted loss or impairment of a body part or organ, or one that requires medical intervention such as surgery, hospitalization or physical rehabilitation.
Automated external defibrillator. Any use on a resident, visitor or staff member on the premises is reportable.

procedures: Immediate response: the staff member who discovers or witnesses an incident first ensures the resident's safety and calls 9-1-1 for any imminent threat to health or life. Staff then give first aid within their training and stay with the resident.

Staff notify the Administrator or the on-call designee ([ADMINISTRATOR NAME], [PHONE]) as soon as the resident is safe, and no later than the end of the shift. For deaths, fires, injuries needing emergency care and suspected abuse, staff call immediately.

The Administrator or designee decides the reporting category (7-day, 24-hour, immediate fire, 2-hour or 24-hour abuse, or financial notice) using the Reporting Timeline Table kept at the front of the incident binder, and records the decision and time on the incident report.

The staff member who witnessed or discovered the incident completes the facility incident report before the end of the shift. It states date, time, place, persons involved, what happened, observations, injuries, first aid or 9-1-1 actions, and witnesses. It records facts only, not opinions.

Fires and explosions: staff call 9-1-1 and the local fire authority immediately. The Administrator notifies the licensing agency by phone or fax no later than the next working day and records the name of the person spoken to and the time.

Outbreaks, poisonings, catastrophes and major accidents: the Administrator calls or faxes the licensing agency and the local health officer ([LOCAL HEALTH OFFICER PHONE]) within 24 hours of discovery and documents the date, time, method and the person contacted. For poisoning the Administrator also follows the poison control instructions given by phone.

Suspected physical abuse of an elder or dependent adult: the Administrator or any mandated reporter follows SP-01. If there is serious bodily injury, the report goes by phone to the local ombudsman, the licensing agency and local law enforcement within 2 hours. Otherwise the report goes within 24 hours. The ombudsman CRISISline is 1-800-231-4024.

The Administrator notifies the person responsible for the resident by phone as soon as possible after any reportable incident and records the time, the person reached and what was said. If the person cannot be reached, the Administrator documents each attempt and keeps trying.

The Administrator submits the written report to the licensing agency and to the person responsible for the resident within 7 days of any death, physician-determined serious injury, AED use, or incident threatening welfare, safety or health. This is done on the licensing agency's current unusual incident/injury report form or an equivalent report with the same content. The Administrator keeps a dated copy and proof of delivery.

A serious injury is determined by the physician. If a resident is injured and no physician has yet assessed the injury, staff arrange assessment, and the Administrator reports within 7 days of the physician's determination or earlier if the injury plainly meets the standard.

After the immediate report, the Administrator reviews the incident within 3 working days, identifies causes, and updates the resident's needs and services plan (AD-02), staffing, environment or training as needed. Findings and corrective actions are recorded on the incident report.

Financial and administrative events: when the facility receives a foreclosure notice, unlawful detainer, bankruptcy filing, rent default notice or utility shut-off notice, the Administrator or owner gives written notice to the licensing agency within 2 business days and keeps a copy with proof of delivery. Applicants are told of any such notice before they sign the admission agreement (RR-03).

Changes in leadership: the Administrator submits written notice of a new administrator to the licensing agency within 30 days, and written notice of a change of chief corporate officer within 15 working days (REC-02).
Follow-up: if the licensing agency, ombudsman or law enforcement requests more information, the Administrator responds promptly, keeps a log of requests and replies, and makes records available.
Quarterly, the Administrator compiles an incident log summary (type, number, time of day, location, report timeliness) and presents it to the governing body for quality review (GOV-03).
All staff are trained on this policy at orientation and annually (ST-03). Training records are kept in personnel files (ST-05).

responsibilities.duty: Decides report category, makes all phone, fax and written reports within the required times, notifies the responsible person, completes follow-up and keeps all copies.
Make the resident safe, call 9-1-1 when needed, notify the Administrator immediately and write the incident report before the end of the shift.
Act as the first contact after hours, make required emergency calls and notify the Administrator without delay.
Provide the Administrator with notices of foreclosure, default, bankruptcy or utility shut-off immediately so that the 2-business-day notice can be met, and review quarterly incident trends.

documentation: Facility incident report for each event, with date and time of discovery and of each notification
Written 7-day report to the licensing agency and the person responsible for the resident, with proof of delivery
Phone or fax log for 24-hour, fire and abuse reports, showing the name of the person contacted, date, time and method
Copy of the 2-business-day financial notice and the proof of delivery
Quarterly incident summary and governing body review minutes
Training attendance records on incident reporting

policies.title: Elopement and Missing Resident
policies.applies_to: All staff and volunteers of [AGENCY NAME], the Administrator and the on-call designee
policies.purpose: To protect residents who may leave the facility unsafely, while respecting the right of every resident to come and go, and to ensure that a missing resident is found quickly and the event is reported as California requires.
policies.policy: Residents of [AGENCY NAME] may leave at any time and may not be locked in (22 CCR §87468.1). The facility does not use locks, barriers or other means that prevent a resident from leaving. We manage wandering and elopement risk through appraisal, supervision, a safe environment and prompt response. At the pre-admission appraisal and each reappraisal, we identify residents at risk of wandering or leaving unsafely (AD-01). We provide awake night supervision when a resident with dementia needs it, based on appraisal, reappraisal or observation (22 CCR §87705). Night supervision meets 22 CCR §87415: for fewer than 16 residents, a qualified person on call on the premises overnight, and awake staff whenever §87705 requires it; for 16 to 100 residents, one employee awake on duty plus one on call within 10 minutes. Night staff must know the emergency plan and be trained in first aid. When a resident cannot be found, staff search immediately, call law enforcement, and notify the person responsible for the resident. An unexplained absence is reported in writing to the licensing agency and the person responsible within 7 days (22 CCR §87211).

definitions.definition: A resident leaving the facility or its grounds without staff knowledge, in a way that places the resident at risk, such as a resident with dementia who cannot find the way back.
A resident whose whereabouts are not known after a quick check of the usual places, regardless of the resident's right to go out.
A resident's departure that the resident or the responsible person has told staff about, with a known destination and expected return.
At least one staff member awake and on duty during sleeping hours.
An absence that staff cannot account for and that threatens the resident's welfare, safety or health; it is a reportable incident under 22 CCR §87211.

procedures: At pre-admission appraisal and at each reappraisal, the Administrator or designee asks the resident and the responsible person about wandering, exit-seeking, past elopement, disorientation and unsafe behavior and records the answers (AD-01).

Residents identified as at risk have an individualized plan in the needs and services plan (AD-02). It covers supervision level, interventions that do not restrict leaving, and a current photo and description kept in the resident record.

The Administrator decides at admission and each reappraisal whether a resident with dementia needs awake night supervision. When this is needed, an awake night staff person is scheduled every night, even in a home with fewer than 16 residents (22 CCR §87705; ST-01).

The facility staffs nights per 22 CCR §87415: a qualified person on call on the premises for fewer than 16 residents; one employee awake on duty plus one on call within 10 minutes for 16 to 100 residents. Night staff are first-aid trained and have been oriented to the emergency plan (SP-05) before working alone.

Staff keep doors unlocked in the direction of exit. Door chimes or similar notification devices may be used only if they do not prevent exit and are consistent with the fire clearance and licensing requirements.
Staff do a head count and visual check at each shift change, at each meal and at bedtime, and note residents who leave for outings or visits on the sign-out record.

Residents with capacity may leave on their own. Staff encourage them to say where they are going and when they expect to return, record the information on the sign-out log, and respect the resident's choice.

When any staff member cannot find a resident, the staff member calls out to other staff and starts the missing-resident response without waiting for permission: one person stays in charge, and the others check the resident's room, bathrooms, common areas, outside areas, vehicles and nearby places the resident knows.

If the resident is not found in the quick check, or the resident is a person with dementia, or the weather, time of day or health condition raises the risk, staff call 9-1-1 and report a missing elder immediately. They give the resident's name, description, photo, clothing, medical conditions and last known time and place.

Staff notify the Administrator or on-call designee ([ADMINISTRATOR NAME], [PHONE]) immediately. The Administrator directs the search, assigns one staff member to the phone and ensures that remaining residents are supervised.

The Administrator or designee notifies the person responsible for the resident as soon as the search starts and updates that person until the resident is found. Calls are recorded with time, person reached and content.

When the resident is found, staff check the resident for injury and call 9-1-1 if needed, return the resident safely, notify law enforcement, the Administrator and the responsible person, and arrange physician notification (HS-03).

The Administrator submits the written report of the unexplained absence to the licensing agency and the person responsible within 7 days (22 CCR §87211; SP-02). If the resident is injured or dies, the Administrator makes the additional reports required by SP-02.

Within 3 working days, the Administrator reviews the event with staff, identifies how the resident left, and updates the needs and services plan, supervision, staffing and environment. Findings are recorded.

All staff are trained on this policy at orientation and annually, including recognition of wandering behavior and the missing-resident response. Staff practice the missing-resident response at least [ELOPEMENT DRILL FREQUENCY], and records are kept.
Because residents have the right to leave and to refuse care (22 CCR §87468.1), staff never physically restrain a resident, lock a door or take away shoes or clothing to prevent leaving (SP-04).

responsibilities.duty: Identifies at-risk residents, schedules awake night supervision where needed, directs the search, notifies the responsible person, makes the written report and reviews the event.
Know which residents are at risk, do headcounts and checks, begin the search at once and call 9-1-1.
Remain awake when required, know the emergency plan, hold first-aid training and make the first calls overnight.
Updates the needs and services plan and reappraises residents after any elopement or near miss.

documentation: Appraisal and reappraisal notes on wandering and elopement risk
Current photo and description for each at-risk resident
Sign-out log and headcount records
Night staffing schedule showing awake staff
Missing-resident incident report, search log and call records
Written 7-day report to the licensing agency and responsible person
Post-incident review and plan updates
Training and drill records

policies.title: Restraints, Postural Supports and Restrictive Practices
policies.applies_to: All staff and volunteers of [AGENCY NAME], the Administrator and contracted health professionals
policies.purpose: To protect residents from restraint, punishment, humiliation and intimidation, to limit any postural support to what the Department's regulations allow, and to ensure that any restrictive intervention is documented and reviewed.
policies.policy: Residents of [AGENCY NAME] are free from punishment, humiliation, intimidation and abuse, may refuse care and may leave at any time, and cannot be locked in (22 CCR §87468.1). Staff do not use restraints to control behavior or for staff convenience. We do not lock residents in rooms or the building, tie or hold residents down, use seclusion, or withhold food, visits or personal items as discipline. Staff never force, hide or camouflage medications (22 CCR §87465). Giving medication in a manner that makes a resident drowsy or quiet for staff convenience is a prohibited chemical restraint. Postural supports, when needed to improve a resident's posture or position, are used only as the Department's regulations on postural supports permit and only on a written physician order. Our staff receive 4 hours of training on postural supports, restricted conditions and hospice within the initial 20 hours before working alone (HSC §1569.625) and refresher training in annual training. Any restrictive intervention is documented and reviewed with the physician and the person responsible for the resident.

definitions.definition: Any device, garment, material or hold that restricts a resident's freedom of movement or normal access to the body and that the resident cannot easily remove.
A device used to achieve proper body position, balance or alignment so a resident can function safely, used only as the Department's regulations allow and under physician order.

Use of a medication to control or sedate a resident for staff convenience or discipline rather than for a diagnosed condition under a physician order. This includes forcing, hiding or camouflaging medication.
Any action that limits a resident's movement, choice, access to belongings or personal rights, including locked doors, seclusion, removal of mobility aids and restriction of visitors.
The resident's authorized representative or family member named in the resident record.

procedures: All staff are told at orientation that restraints, seclusion, punishment, humiliation and intimidation are prohibited, and that residents may refuse care and may leave (22 CCR §87468.1). Staff sign an acknowledgment kept in the personnel file (ST-05).

Staff use person-centered, non-restrictive responses first: redirection, stopping and reapproaching later, offering choices, addressing pain, hunger, toileting and other unmet needs, and calling the Administrator.

Staff do not lock a resident in or out of any room or area, do not take away mobility aids, glasses, hearing aids or shoes, and do not use bed rails, tie-downs, lap trays or chairs that the resident cannot leave unless they qualify as a postural support under the next steps.

A postural support may be considered only when the resident's physician orders it in writing and the Department's regulations on postural supports are met. The Administrator confirms the order, the device type, the purpose and the conditions before the device is used.

The Administrator contacts the physician and the person responsible for the resident before first use, explains the reason, alternatives tried and the risks, and records the discussion and the agreement of the resident or responsible person.

The needs and services plan (AD-02) is updated to include the postural support, its purpose, how and when it is applied and checked, and who will review it. If the resident's needs go beyond what the facility may lawfully provide, the Administrator begins the retention review under AD-03.
Trained staff apply and check the device as ordered. Staff check the resident at the frequency stated in the plan, ensure comfort, skin condition, circulation and toileting, and record each check.

The resident can ask for the device to be removed at any time. Staff remove it when the resident asks unless the physician's order and the plan require otherwise for immediate safety, and they notify the Administrator.

Staff never force, hide or camouflage medications. If a resident refuses a medication, staff do not insist and instead record the refusal and notify the physician or responsible person as set out in HS-01 and HS-02.

If any staff member sees or suspects a restraint, use of force or other restrictive practice outside this policy, the staff member stops it, makes sure the resident is safe and tells the Administrator at once. Suspected abuse is reported under SP-01.

The Administrator documents any restrictive intervention on an incident report, including the reason, alternatives tried, duration, resident's response and persons notified, and reviews it with the physician and the person responsible for the resident within [REVIEW INTERVAL, e.g., 30 days] of first use and at every reappraisal.
Postural supports and other restrictive interventions are reviewed at each reappraisal to see if they are still needed, and are discontinued when no longer needed.

New direct care staff complete the 4 hours of postural supports, restricted conditions and hospice training within their first 20 hours, before working alone, and receive refresher training in annual training (HSC §1569.625; ST-03).
Staff who use a prohibited restraint or any punishment, humiliation or intimidation are subject to discipline up to termination and are reported as required (SP-01; ST-06).
The Administrator reviews restraint and restriction practices and any incidents annually with the governing body (GOV-03).

responsibilities.duty: Enforces the prohibition, verifies physician orders and conditions for postural supports, updates plans, reviews interventions with the physician and responsible person and handles discipline.
Use non-restrictive approaches, apply and check ordered supports as trained, record checks and report any restrictive practice.
Evaluates the need for a postural support, issues the written order and reviews it at reassessment.
Receives explanation, takes part in decisions and is notified of any restrictive intervention.

documentation: Staff acknowledgment of the restraint prohibition
Written physician order for any postural support
Needs and services plan entries and reappraisal notes
Resident or responsible person consent or agreement and notification records
Check logs for each use of a postural support
Incident report and review of any restrictive intervention
Training records for the 4-hour postural supports/restricted conditions/hospice topic and annual refreshers

policies.title: Emergency Preparedness and Disaster Plan
policies.applies_to: All staff and volunteers of [AGENCY NAME], the Administrator and the governing body
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] has a written, tested disaster and mass casualty plan that protects residents during fire, earthquake, flood, power loss, public health emergency and other emergencies, and that all staff, including night staff, know their role.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] keeps a written disaster and mass casualty plan (Emergency Disaster Plan, LIC 610E) that is readily available to staff at all times, as required by 22 CCR §87212. The plan sets out: administrative authority and staff assignments; the fire safety plan; means of exiting; assembly at a predetermined evacuation site; transportation; relocation sites equipped for safe temporary accommodation; supervision of residents during evacuation and contact after relocation; contact with fire, law enforcement and disaster agencies; and notification of a resident's hospice agency on evacuation or relocation. Emergency exit plans and emergency telephone numbers are posted. Night staff know the emergency plan and are trained in first aid (22 CCR §87415). Fire clearance is in place before licensure, and a separate fire clearance is in place before the facility accepts or keeps any nonambulatory or bedridden resident (22 CCR §87202).

definitions.definition: The facility's written disaster and mass casualty plan under 22 CCR §87212.
The predetermined safe place near the facility where residents and staff gather after leaving the building.
A pre-arranged location equipped to house residents safely for a temporary stay when the facility cannot be occupied.
A resident who cannot leave the building without help from another person, or who is confined to bed; a separate fire clearance is required to serve such residents.
An event that injures or endangers several residents or staff at one time and requires outside emergency help.

procedures: Before opening, the Administrator completes the Emergency Disaster Plan (LIC 610E) with all elements required by 22 CCR §87212 and submits it with the application (SA-05). The plan is approved by the owner or governing body.

The plan names the administrative authority and staff assignments for each emergency role (incident lead, resident evacuation, head count, phone and agency contact, first aid, medications and records) and names a substitute for each role on every shift.
The plan includes the fire safety plan, exit routes from every room, and the means of exiting for ambulatory and nonambulatory residents (SP-06).
The plan names the predetermined evacuation site, with address and walking route, and a second site if the first cannot be used.
The plan names transportation for evacuating all residents, including those with wheelchairs, walkers or oxygen, with the provider's name and phone ([TRANSPORTATION PROVIDER PHONE]), and a back-up.

The plan names at least one relocation site that is equipped for safe temporary accommodation (beds, food, water, toileting, medication storage and electrical needs). The site's name, address, phone and written agreement are kept with the plan: [RELOCATION SITE NAME, ADDRESS, PHONE].

The plan describes how residents are supervised during evacuation and how staff and families keep in contact with each resident after relocation, including a resident tracking list with name, photo, medications, diagnoses and responsible person's phone number.

The plan lists emergency contacts: fire department, law enforcement, disaster agencies, the licensing agency, the local health officer, the ombudsman and utilities, with phone numbers ([FIRE DEPARTMENT PHONE], [LAW ENFORCEMENT PHONE], [LOCAL OFFICE OF EMERGENCY SERVICES PHONE]).
The plan requires staff to notify a resident's hospice agency whenever a hospice resident is evacuated or relocated, and to give the agency the new location and contact number (HS-06).

The plan and a map of exits are kept in the office and in [PLAN LOCATION] where all staff can reach them at any time, including nights. Emergency exit plans and emergency telephone numbers are posted in [POSTING LOCATIONS], where residents and visitors can see them.
